fuentes/naufrago/resumen.texto: Middle Kingdom tale in which a sailor tells a dejected official how he was shipwrecked on an island after a voyage to the king's mines, and met a talking serpent who says he is lord of Punt. The only manuscript is from the Twelfth Dynasty.

fuentes/naufrago/por_que_importa.texto: It is an example of the Middle Kingdom adventure tale, and it mentions Red Sea expeditions, which are associated with trade with Punt.

fuentes/campesino-elocuente/resumen.texto: A peasant who is robbed by an official presents nine eloquent petitions before a high official until he obtains justice. It is set in the First Intermediate Period, under Herakleopolitan kings, and it was written in the Middle Kingdom.

fuentes/campesino-elocuente/por_que_impo.texto: It shows the idea of justice (maat) in Middle Kingdom literature and its models of rhetoric.

fuentes/instrucciones-de-amenemhat/resum.texto: Wisdom text written as if dictated by King Amenemhat I from the afterlife to his son Senusret I, with an account of a nighttime attack against the king. It survives mainly in New Kingdom copies.

fuentes/instrucciones-de-amenemhat/por_q.texto: It is one of the few sources on the end of Amenemhat I, although its literary character keeps it from being taken as a chronicle.

fuentes/profecia-de-neferti/soporte.texto: Hieratic papyrus (St. Petersburg 1116B) and other copies

fuentes/profecia-de-neferti/resumen.texto: The priest Neferti predicts before Snefru a time of disorder and announces the coming of a southern king named Ameny, who is usually identified with Amenemhat I. The work was composed under the Twelfth Dynasty, although it is set in the Old Kingdom.

fuentes/profecia-de-neferti/por_que_impo.texto: It is considered a legitimizing text for Amenemhat I, although the date of its composition is debated.

fuentes/admoniciones-de-ipuur/resumen.texto: Speech by a sage, Ipuwer, before a king about a land in disorder: reversal of ranks, famine, and violence. The only manuscript is a copy from the Nineteenth Dynasty; the date of composition is debated between the Middle Kingdom, which many authors maintain, and the Second Intermediate Period, and its historical setting is linked to the First Intermediate Period.

fuentes/admoniciones-de-ipuur/por_que_im.texto: It has been read as testimony to the end of the Old Kingdom and as a literary work that does not describe a specific event; the debate over its date affects that reading.

fuentes/disputa-de-un-hombre-con-su-ba/t.texto: Dispute Between a Man and His Ba

fuentes/disputa-de-un-hombre-con-su-ba/r.texto: Dialogue in which a man, weary of life, argues with his ba about whether he should die. The manuscript, from the Twelfth Dynasty, is incomplete.

fuentes/disputa-de-un-hombre-con-su-ba/p.texto: It is one of the earliest Egyptian reflections on suicide and death, and it is studied for its poetic form.

fuentes/satira-de-los-oficios/titulo.texto: Satire of the Trades (Instruction of Kheti)

fuentes/satira-de-los-oficios/soporte.texto: Sallier II Papyrus (BM EA 10182) and other New Kingdom copies on papyri and ostraca

fuentes/satira-de-los-oficios/resumen.texto: Instruction that the scribe Kheti, of Sile, gives to his son Pepi, whom he takes to the scribal school and to whom he compares the hardships of the other trades with the life of the scribe. It was composed in the Middle Kingdom, the complete text is in the Sallier II Papyrus, and Egyptologists debate whether it is satirical.

fuentes/satira-de-los-oficios/por_que_im.texto: It shows how manual labor was seen from the position of the official, and it was a school copying text for centuries.

fuentes/amduat/soporte.texto: Paintings and reliefs in royal tombs of the Valley of the Kings

fuentes/amduat/resumen.texto: “Book of What Is in the Afterlife,” which describes the sun's nightly journey through the twelve hours of the underworld. There are fragments in KV20, KV38, and the tomb of Thutmose II (Wadi C-4), and the first complete version is in KV34, of Thutmose III.

fuentes/amduat/por_que_importa.texto: It is the main royal funerary text of the New Kingdom and gives the image of the underworld that the kings used.

fuentes/papiro-de-ani/resumen.texto: Illustrated copy of the Book of the Dead written for the scribe Ani, of the Nineteenth Dynasty, which contains the scene of the weighing of the heart. It was compiled for a Theban scribe.

fuentes/papiro-de-ani/por_que_importa.texto: It is the best-known copy of the Book of the Dead and shows its Ramesside form.

fuentes/papiro-rhind/resumen.texto: Collection of problems and calculation tables copied by the scribe Ahmes in year 33 of King Auserre, who is identified with Apepi of the Fifteenth Dynasty, c. 1550 BC. The text itself says that he copies an original from the time of Nimaatre, that is, Amenemhat III.

fuentes/papiro-rhind/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the two main sources of Egyptian mathematics, and its double date, of copy and of original, illustrates the problem of dating papyri.

fuentes/papiro-matematico-de-moscu/resum.texto: Papyrus with twenty-five calculation problems, among them the volume of a truncated pyramid, from the late Twelfth or early Thirteenth Dynasty. Golenishchev bought it, and it is in Moscow.

fuentes/papiro-matematico-de-moscu/por_q.texto: It is older than the Rhind Papyrus and shows the level of Egyptian mathematics before the Hyksos.

fuentes/papiros-de-kahun/soporte.texto: Papyri found at Lahun by Petrie in 1889

fuentes/papiros-de-kahun/resumen.texto: Set of Middle Kingdom papyri found in the workers' town of Lahun, with administrative records, letters, medical and veterinary texts, and contracts. It includes the Kahun Gynaecological Papyrus.

fuentes/papiros-de-kahun/por_que_importa.texto: They inform us about life in a Middle Kingdom town and about the medicine of the period.

fuentes/textos-de-execracion/resumen.texto: Names of enemies of Egypt, Nubians, Libyans, and Asiatics, written on clay figurines or vessels that were broken in a ritual. The Middle Kingdom texts bear the names of cities and chiefs of the Levant.

fuentes/textos-de-execracion/por_que_imp.texto: They are an early source for the political geography of the Levant and for the Egyptian attitude toward its neighbors.

fuentes/anales-de-tutmosis-iii/soporte.texto: Inscriptions on the walls of the temple of Amun at Karnak

fuentes/anales-de-tutmosis-iii/resumen.texto: Account on the walls of the Karnak temple of Thutmose III's campaigns in Asia, supposedly compiled from war diaries. It recounts the battle of Megiddo in year 23 and the tribute of the campaigns that followed.

fuentes/anales-de-tutmosis-iii/por_que_i.texto: It is the main source on the pharaoh's campaigns and on the geography of the Levant in the mid-15th century BC.

fuentes/anales-de-tutmosis-iii/leer.0.ti.texto: Translation by Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 2 (1906)

fuentes/papiro-harris-i/soporte.texto: Papyrus about forty-one meters long (British Museum)

fuentes/papiro-harris-i/resumen.texto: The longest surviving papyrus from Egypt, written under Ramesses IV, lists Ramesses III's donations to the temples of Egypt and ends with a summary of his reign. It mentions the defeat of the Sea Peoples and a period of disorder before Setnakht.

fuentes/papiro-harris-i/por_que_importa.texto: It gives the official Egyptian view of the end of the Nineteenth Dynasty and of the reign of Ramesses III.

fuentes/papiro-harris-i/leer.0.titulo.texto: Translation by Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 4 (1906)

fuentes/papiro-de-la-huelga-de-turin/res.texto: Record by a scribe of Deir el-Medina of the events of year 29 of Ramesses III, when the necropolis workers stopped work for lack of grain rations and marched toward Thebes. Some authors consider it the first documented labor strike in history.

fuentes/papiro-de-la-huelga-de-turin/por.texto: It is the main source on the strike and on the administration of the tomb workers.

fuentes/papiro-judicial-de-turin/resumen.texto: Record of the trial of the accused in the harem conspiracy against Ramesses III, with the lists of the condemned, under changed names, and the sentences. It also mentions judges who were later condemned for dealings with the women involved.

fuentes/papiro-judicial-de-turin/por_que.texto: It is the main document on the assassination attempt and on New Kingdom judicial procedures.

fuentes/papiro-judicial-de-turin/leer.0..texto: Translation by Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 4 (1906)

fuentes/papiro-leopold-ii-amherst/soport.texto: Papyrus, in two parts (Brussels and New York)

fuentes/papiro-leopold-ii-amherst/resume.texto: Part of the judicial records on tomb robberies under Ramesses IX, from year 16 of the king, containing the confessions of eight men who entered the tomb of Sobekemsaf II and the reconstruction of the crime.

fuentes/papiro-leopold-ii-amherst/por_qu.texto: It complements the Abbott Papyrus with testimony from the thieves and shows how Ramesside justice worked.

fuentes/papiro-leopold-ii-amherst/leer.0.texto: Translation by Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 4 (1906), which covers only the Amherst part of the papyrus

fuentes/papiro-salt-124/resumen.texto: Accusation against the foreman Paneb of Deir el-Medina for theft, abuse, and violence, presented before the vizier under Seti II. The verdict is not preserved.

fuentes/papiro-salt-124/por_que_importa.texto: It is a source on the internal conflicts of the village of the workers of the royal tombs.

fuentes/papiro-wilbour/resumen.texto: Land register of cultivated fields from Middle Egypt, from year 4 of Ramesses V, with the plots and their managers. It is the most extensive document of its type that survives.

fuentes/papiro-wilbour/por_que_importa.texto: It shows the ownership of land by temples and officials at the end of the New Kingdom.

fuentes/canon-real-de-turin/resumen.texto: List of kings in hieratic script from the Nineteenth Dynasty, with the name and years of reign of each, attributed to the time of Ramesses II. Drovetti bought it in Thebes around 1818, and it reached Italy in fragments, with gaps; where it was written is unknown.

fuentes/canon-real-de-turin/por_que_impo.texto: It is the basis of Egyptian chronology before Ramesses II and the main source for ordering the Thirteenth to Seventeenth Dynasties, although its fragments are hard to place.

fuentes/lista-real-de-abidos/soporte.texto: Relief in the temple of Seti I at Abydos

fuentes/lista-real-de-abidos/resumen.texto: List of seventy-six kings from Menes to Seti I, carved in the temple of Seti I and his son Ramesses II. It omits the kings of the intermediate periods, Hatshepsut, and the kings of Amarna.

fuentes/lista-real-de-abidos/por_que_imp.texto: It shows which kings the official tradition of the Nineteenth Dynasty considered legitimate.

fuentes/lista-de-karnak/soporte.texto: Relief in the temple of Karnak (now in the Louvre)

fuentes/lista-de-karnak/resumen.texto: List of sixty-one kings from Snefru, carved in the Festival Hall of Thutmose III at Karnak. It is badly damaged and is preserved in the Louvre.

fuentes/lista-de-karnak/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the royal lists of the New Kingdom, together with those of Abydos and the Turin Canon.

fuentes/dos-hermanos/resumen.texto: Tale of two brothers, Anubis and Bata, with the slander by the elder's wife, Bata's transformation and his death and resurrection. The papyrus was copied by the scribe Ennana under Seti II.

fuentes/dos-hermanos/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the best-preserved folk tales of the New Kingdom.

fuentes/dos-hermanos/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation on Wikisource (Egyptian Literature, “Anpu and Bata”)

fuentes/principe-predestinado/resumen.texto: Incomplete tale of a prince to whom the Hathors announce that he will die from a crocodile, a snake, or a dog, and who travels to Syria. The ending is not preserved.

fuentes/principe-predestinado/por_que_im.texto: It is one of the few New Kingdom tales with a destiny and a journey abroad.

fuentes/principe-predestinado/leer.0.tit.texto: English translation on Wikisource (Egyptian Literature, “The Doomed Prince”)

fuentes/contiendas-de-horus-y-seth/resum.texto: Account of the dispute before the court of the gods over the succession of Osiris, with comic episodes. The papyrus belongs to the Twentieth Dynasty, and its editors date it under Ramesses V.

fuentes/contiendas-de-horus-y-seth/por_q.texto: It is the best-preserved version of that mythical dispute and is written in Ramesside language.

fuentes/instrucciones-de-ani/resumen.texto: Wisdom text attributed to the scribe Ani, with advice on conduct and piety for his son. It is supposed to have been composed in the Eighteenth Dynasty, and the main manuscript is from the Twenty-first Dynasty.

fuentes/instrucciones-de-ani/por_que_imp.texto: It is a source on the everyday morality of the New Kingdom scribe.

fuentes/instruccion-de-amenemope/resumen.texto: Thirty chapters of advice from the scribe Amenemope to his son. The main manuscript is later than the end of the New Kingdom, and the composition is placed between the Nineteenth and the Twenty-first Dynasties. Since Erman (1924) there has been an almost general consensus that Proverbs 22:17-24:22 depends on Amenemope.

fuentes/instruccion-de-amenemope/por_que.texto: It is the Egyptian wisdom work most often compared with the Bible.

fuentes/viaje-de-unamon/resumen.texto: First-person account by an official from Karnak sent to Byblos to buy cedar wood for the barque of Amun, who suffers theft and slights. It is usually dated to year 5 of the “Renaissance era,” under Ramesses XI, but the date has been debated since Jansen-Winkeln reversed the order of Herihor and Piankh. The papyrus appeared at el-Hiba together with the Onomastica of Amenope and the Tale of Misfortune. It is debated whether it is an official report or a tale.

fuentes/viaje-de-unamon/por_que_importa.texto: It shows the loss of Egyptian prestige on the Levantine coast.

fuentes/viaje-de-unamon/leer.0.titulo.texto: Translation by Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 4 (1906)

fuentes/papiro-anastasi-i/resumen.texto: Satirical letter between two scribes with a tour of the cities and routes of Syria and Palestine. It gives place names such as Megiddo and Byblos.

fuentes/papiro-anastasi-i/por_que_import.texto: It is a source for the geography of the Levant in the time of Ramesses II.

fuentes/autobiografia-de-ahmose-hijo-de-.texto: Autobiography of Ahmose son of Ebana
Inscription in his tomb at El Kab

Text in the tomb of Ahmose, sailor and soldier, recounting his service under Ahmose I, Amenhotep I, and Thutmose I. It narrates the siege of Avaris, the capture of Sharuhen, and the campaigns in Nubia and Syria.
It is the source closest to the expulsion of the Hyksos and to the campaigns of the Eighteenth Dynasty.
Translation by Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 2 (1906)

fuentes/autobiografia-de-ahmose-pennejbe.texto: Inscription in his tomb at El Kab
Text in tomb EK2 of a soldier from El Kab who served under Ahmose I and continued with every king up to Thutmose III. It recounts campaigns in northern Canaan, Nubia, Naharin, and Sinai.
It complements the autobiography of Ahmose son of Ebana for the campaigns of the early Eighteenth Dynasty.
Translation by Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 2 (1906)

fuentes/estelas-de-kamose/soporte.texto: Stelae from Karnak (the second) and a wooden tablet

fuentes/estelas-de-kamose/resumen.texto: Texts of two stelae that show Kamose in council with his courtiers, who dissuade him from attacking the Hyksos, and his campaign against Apepi. They narrate his advance as far as Neferusi and the interception of a messenger that Apepi was sending to the ruler of Kush.

fuentes/estelas-de-kamose/por_que_import.texto: They are the most direct account of the beginnings of the war of liberation.

fuentes/tablilla-carnarvon/resumen.texto: Wooden school tablet of the Eighteenth Dynasty with a copy of the first stela of Kamose, found by Carnarvon in 1908 near the entrance of a tomb in the Valley of Deir el-Bahari. It is the most complete copy of the beginning of the first stela; the reverse has the beginning of the Instruction of Ptahhotep.

fuentes/tablilla-carnarvon/por_que_impor.texto: It preserves the beginning of Kamose's narrative, which the stela lost.

fuentes/estela-de-restauracion/resumen.texto: Stela of Tutankhamun that says that, before his reign, the temples were in ruins and the gods did not listen, and that the king restored the cult and its endowments. It does not name Akhenaten.

fuentes/estela-de-restauracion/por_que_i.texto: It is the text used to document the end of Atenism.

fuentes/tumba-de-rejmira/titulo.texto: Inscriptions in the tomb of Rekhmire

fuentes/tumba-de-rejmira/soporte.texto: Paintings and inscriptions of the Theban tomb TT100

fuentes/tumba-de-rejmira/resumen.texto: Paintings in the tomb of the vizier Rekhmire with scenes of craftsmen and tribute from Punt, Crete, Nubia, and Syria, and the text of the “Installation of the Vizier,” which sets out his duties.

fuentes/tumba-de-rejmira/por_que_importa.texto: It informs us about the administration of Thutmose III and the tribute of foreign countries.

fuentes/tumba-de-rejmira/leer.0.titulo.texto: Translation by Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 2 (1906)

fuentes/estela-del-sueno/soporte.texto: Granite stela between the paws of the Sphinx

fuentes/estela-del-sueno/resumen.texto: Stela of Thutmose IV at Giza, in which the king tells that, as a prince, he dreamed that the Sphinx promised him the throne if he uncovered it. It documents the clearing of the monument.

fuentes/estela-del-sueno/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the sources on his accession to the throne and on the cult of the Sphinx in the New Kingdom.

fuentes/estela-del-sueno/leer.0.titulo.texto: Translation by Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 2 (1906)

fuentes/papiros-de-heqanakht/soporte.texto: Papyri found in the funerary complex of the vizier Ipi, at Deir el-Bahari (Metropolitan Museum)

fuentes/papiros-de-heqanakht/resumen.texto: Letters and accounts of a ka priest, Heqanakht, who writes from the Theban region to his family, who lived far from him, with instructions on rations and rents. According to one reading the family was near the capital, next to the Faiyum, and other authors (James P. Allen) reverse the location; they are dated to the beginning of the Twelfth Dynasty.

fuentes/papiros-de-heqanakht/por_que_imp.texto: They offer a portrait of a Middle Kingdom family of landholders, with its finances and conflicts.

fuentes/ryholt-1997/titulo.texto: The Political Situation in Egypt during the Second Intermediate Period, c. 1800-1550 BC

fuentes/ryholt-1997/resumen.texto: Study of the Thirteenth to Seventeenth Dynasties that reconstructs, from the Turin Canon, the list of kings and reigns of the Second Intermediate Period. It proposes the founding of the Fourteenth Dynasty in the Delta and orders the Sixteenth and Seventeenth. Published by Museum Tusculanum Press, Copenhagen (CNI Publications 20).

fuentes/ryholt-1997/por_que_importa.texto: It is the reference for the chronologies of kings of that period. Its reconstruction, especially of the Fourteenth and Sixteenth Dynasties, is disputed by Ben-Tor, on the basis of scarab seriation, and by Bietak.

fuentes/grajetzki-reino-medio/titulo.texto: The Middle Kingdom of Ancient Egypt: History, Archaeology and Society

fuentes/grajetzki-reino-medio/resumen.texto: Synthesis of the Middle Kingdom, of the Eleventh to Thirteenth Dynasties, with its kings, tombs, and the functioning of society. It covers the debate on coregencies and dates.

fuentes/grajetzki-reino-medio/por_que_im.texto: It is a current introduction to the Middle Kingdom.

fuentes/redford-egypt-canaan-israel/titu.texto: Egypt, Canaan, and Israel in Ancient Times

fuentes/redford-egypt-canaan-israel/resu.texto: History of Egypt's relations with the Levant and Palestine, from Egyptian campaign inscriptions to the Amarna texts and the stela of Merneptah. It discusses Egyptian rule in Canaan in the New Kingdom.

fuentes/redford-egypt-canaan-israel/por_.texto: It is a reference for Egypt's Asiatic policy.

fuentes/cline-1177/resumen.texto: Study of the collapse of the civilizations of the eastern Mediterranean around 1200 BC, which reviews Ramesses III's campaigns against the Sea Peoples and the explanations proposed: earthquakes, droughts, invasions, and failures of trade.

fuentes/cline-1177/por_que_importa.texto: It sums up the debate on the end of the Bronze Age and Egypt's place in it.

fuentes/kitchen-ramesside-inscriptions/r.texto: Edition in hieroglyphs, in eight published volumes by B. H. Blackwell, Oxford, of the historical and biographical inscriptions of the 19th and 20th Dynasties; the first volume is from 1975. It is the reference edition for Seti I, Ramesses II, Merenptah and the kings of the 20th Dynasty; the English translation is a separate series (Ramesside Inscriptions, Translated and Annotated).

fuentes/kitchen-ramesside-inscriptions/p.texto: It is the basis of modern translations of Ramesside texts.

fuentes/the-architecture-of-imperialism/.texto: The Architecture of Imperialism: Military Bases and the Evolution of Foreign Policy in Egypt's New Kingdom
Study of Egypt's fortresses and military bases in Canaan and Nubia in the New Kingdom and their relation to foreign policy. It combines texts and excavations.
It is a reference on Egyptian domination in Asia and Nubia.

fuentes/papiro-hearst/soporte.texto: Papyrus of the University of California

fuentes/papiro-hearst/resumen.texto: Medical papyrus of the 18th Dynasty with recipes and remedies, which Reisner acquired for the Hearst expedition in 1901. It has affinities with the Ebers Papyrus.

fuentes/papiro-hearst/por_que_importa.texto: It is a source on New Kingdom Egyptian medicine, complementary to Ebers and Edwin Smith.

fuentes/papiros-mayer/resumen.texto: Two documents of the 20th Dynasty containing court records. Mayer Papyrus A records the sessions of the first two years of the “Renaissance era”, from year 19 of Ramesses XI, when a court interrogated suspects in tomb robbery at Deir el-Bahari and acquitted five of them. It is dated to c. 1083–1080 BC.

fuentes/papiros-mayer/por_que_importa.texto: It shows how Ramesside justice worked and complements the Abbott and Amherst papyri.

fuentes/papiro-dramatico-del-ramesseum/s.texto: Papyrus roll (British Museum), found in the Ramesseum

fuentes/papiro-dramatico-del-ramesseum/r.texto: The oldest surviving illustrated scroll. It contains a ceremonial work for the coronation or the Sed festival of Senusret I, of the 12th Dynasty, in linear hieroglyphs, with the scenes below the text as in a comic strip and the king in the role of Horus.

fuentes/papiro-dramatico-del-ramesseum/p.texto: It is one of the few sources for a dramatized ritual of the Middle Kingdom.

fuentes/anales-de-amenemhat-ii/soporte.texto: Fragments of an inscription found at Memphis

fuentes/anales-de-amenemhat-ii/resumen.texto: Fragments found at Memphis of the annals of the reign of Amenemhat II. They record the sending of a mission to the Lebanon region, expeditions to Sinai and, in column 18, the destruction of the Asiatic cities of Iuai and Iasy and the transfer of 1554 prisoners to Egypt; Helck identifies Iasy with Alasia (Cyprus) and Iuai with Ura, in Turkey.

fuentes/anales-de-amenemhat-ii/por_que_i.texto: It is a historical document of the reign and of the conception of kingship in the Middle Kingdom, before the campaigns of Senusret III.

fuentes/estela-de-sebek-khu/soporte.texto: Stela found by Garstang in 1901 next to the tomb of Sebek-khu at Abydos (Manchester Museum)

fuentes/estela-de-sebek-khu/resumen.texto: Stela in honor of Sebek-khu, who lived under Senusret III, with an account of his life. It tells that the king marched against the Asiatics and that Sekmem, identified with Shechem, fell together with the wretched Retenu; it is considered the earliest known record of an Egyptian campaign in Canaan.

fuentes/estela-de-sebek-khu/por_que_impo.texto: It is the main Egyptian source on a campaign in the Levant before the Hyksos.

fuentes/estela-de-sebek-khu/leer.0.titul.texto: Breasted's translation, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 1 (1906)

fuentes/estela-de-ikhernofret/soporte.texto: Limestone stela one metre high (Berlin Museum, 1204)

fuentes/estela-de-ikhernofret/resumen.texto: Stela of twenty-four lines of text that describes in veiled terms how the mysteries of Osiris were celebrated at Abydos. Osiris appears under a winged sun disk before Senusret III, and Ikhernofret, his treasurer, stands before an offering table with his family.

fuentes/estela-de-ikhernofret/por_que_im.texto: It is the main source on the festivals of Osiris at Abydos in the Middle Kingdom.

fuentes/estela-de-ikhernofret/leer.0.tit.texto: Breasted's translation, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 1 (1906)

fuentes/despachos-de-semna/soporte.texto: Group of papyri (British Museum, AE 10752 and 10771)

fuentes/despachos-de-semna/resumen.texto: A group of papyri recording the movements of people around the fortresses of the Semna gorge and reporting them to an unnamed official in Thebes. Several deal with people arriving to trade and with patrols that found people in the nearby desert.

fuentes/despachos-de-semna/por_que_impor.texto: It is one of the few records that say how the southern frontier fortresses worked and how the Egyptians saw the Nubians.

fuentes/papiros-de-reisner/soporte.texto: Four rolls found by Reisner between 1901 and 1904 in a tomb at Naga ed-Deir

fuentes/papiros-de-reisner/resumen.texto: Four papyrus rolls from the reign of Senusret I, found in a wooden coffin. Reisner I, about 3.5 metres long, includes construction records with the number of workers needed, and records from carpentry workshops and shipyards.

fuentes/papiros-de-reisner/por_que_impor.texto: They report on the organization of state works and workshops in the Middle Kingdom.

fuentes/papiro-ginecologico-de-kahun/res.texto: The oldest surviving medical text from Egypt, from c. 1825 BC, in the 12th Dynasty. It deals with gynaecological health problems, pregnancy, fertility and various treatments.

fuentes/papiro-ginecologico-de-kahun/por.texto: It is a source of Egyptian medicine earlier than the New Kingdom papyri.

fuentes/papiros-matematicos-de-lahun/sop.texto: Six fragments of the Kahun Papyri, found by Petrie

fuentes/papiros-matematicos-de-lahun/res.texto: Six fragments of mathematical texts that form part of the Kahun Papyri, found by Petrie in the workers' town next to the pyramid of Senusret II at Lahun.

fuentes/papiros-matematicos-de-lahun/por.texto: They document Middle Kingdom Egyptian mathematics, earlier than the Rhind Papyrus.

fuentes/papiro-de-berlin-6619/resumen.texto: One of the main sources of Egyptian mathematics, from the 12th or 13th Dynasty. One of its two problems may indicate that the Egyptians knew the Pythagorean theorem.

fuentes/papiro-de-berlin-6619/por_que_im.texto: It complements the Moscow and Rhind papyri in reconstructing Middle Kingdom mathematics.

fuentes/rollo-de-cuero-matematico/soport.texto: Leather roll of 25 by 43 cm (British Museum)

fuentes/rollo-de-cuero-matematico/resume.texto: Leather roll written in hieratic in the Middle Kingdom, which Alexander Henry Rhind bought in 1858 and which was sent to the British Museum in 1864 with the Rhind Papyrus; it was not unrolled until 1927. Specialists date it to the 17th century BC.

fuentes/rollo-de-cuero-matematico/por_qu.texto: It contains calculations with fractions that serve to study Egyptian arithmetic.

fuentes/tablillas-de-ajmim/soporte.texto: Two wooden tablets covered with plaster (Egyptian Museum, Cairo)

fuentes/tablillas-de-ajmim/resumen.texto: Two writing tablets, inscribed on both sides, that solve arithmetic problems. The first has a list of servants and a mathematical text dated to year 38 of an unnamed king; the dating to the beginning of the Middle Kingdom and that regnal year suggest that of Senusret I.

fuentes/tablillas-de-ajmim/por_que_impor.texto: They are evidence of applied arithmetic from the beginning of the 12th Dynasty.

fuentes/ensenanza-leal/soporte.texto: Stela from the middle of the 12th Dynasty and New Kingdom papyri

fuentes/ensenanza-leal/resumen.texto: A wisdom text (sebayt) that stresses loyalty to the pharaoh and the duties of those who serve him. It survives in part on a stela from the middle of the 12th Dynasty and in full on New Kingdom papyrus rolls; its author is uncertain, and without direct evidence the vizier Kairsu has been proposed.

fuentes/ensenanza-leal/por_que_importa.texto: It shows the ideology of loyalty to the crown in Middle Kingdom literature.

fuentes/himno-al-nilo/resumen.texto: Hymn to Hapy, the god of the Nile, that celebrates the flood of the river. It says that offerings are made to him and great festivals established for him, and thanks the river for the crops and the provisions of the temples.

fuentes/himno-al-nilo/por_que_importa.texto: It shows the place of the Nile and its flood in Egyptian religion and agricultural economy.

fuentes/inscripciones-de-wadi-el-hol/sop.texto: Two rock inscriptions in a valley on the road from Farshut, between Thebes and Hiw

fuentes/inscripciones-de-wadi-el-hol/res.texto: Two rock inscriptions in limestone that seem to show some of the oldest examples of phonetic alphabetic writing. John and Deborah Darnell found them in 1993 and in 1999 concluded that they are the oldest known alphabet, from c. 1900–1800 BC.

fuentes/inscripciones-de-wadi-el-hol/por.texto: They are linked to the Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions of Serabit el-Khadim and to the origin of alphabets.

fuentes/papiro-brooklyn-35-1446/resumen.texto: One of the most important administrative documents surviving from the Middle Kingdom, written on both sides. The recto has a list of eighty Egyptians who seem to have fled from a large prison or labour camp; the verso, a list of servants, among them many Asiatics. Wilbour bought it between 1881 and 1896, and Hayes published it in 1955.

fuentes/papiro-brooklyn-35-1446/por_que_.texto: It reports on the presence of Asiatics in Egypt before the Hyksos and on compulsory labour.

fuentes/papiro-boulaq-18/resumen.texto: Administrative document with the accounts of the palace of Thebes in the 13th Dynasty, c. 1750 BC, listing the palace officials and the rations they received day by day. Among them are the vizier Ankhu and Queen Aya.

fuentes/papiro-boulaq-18/por_que_importa.texto: It is a source on the court and the administration of Upper Egypt in the 13th Dynasty.

fuentes/decreto-de-coptos-de-intef/sopor.texto: Hieroglyphic inscription on a wall of the temple of Min at Coptos

fuentes/decreto-de-coptos-de-intef/resum.texto: Ruling by Nubkheperre Intef addressed to the mayor of Coptos, Minemhat, to remove Teti, son of Minhotep, from his post in the temple. Teti was said to have stolen an object from the temple of Min or supported the king's enemies; he lost his offices and his descendants were excluded from them.

fuentes/decreto-de-coptos-de-intef/por_q.texto: It gives the highest regnal year attested for Nubkheperre Intef, year 3, and shows the Theban administration of the 17th Dynasty.

fuentes/estela-juridica/soporte.texto: Limestone stela 1.18 m high, with 28 lines (Cairo Museum, JE 52453)

fuentes/estela-juridica/resumen.texto: Stela of year 1 of the Theban king Nebiryraw I, found in 1927 in the Hypostyle Hall of Karnak. It records the sale of the office of governor of El Kab by Kebsi to his relative Sobeknakht, who was collecting a debt of 60 deben of gold.

fuentes/estela-juridica/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the best-known administrative documents of the Second Intermediate Period and shows how offices were passed on.

fuentes/disputa-de-apofis-y-seqenenre/ti.texto: The Quarrel of Apophis and Seqenenre

fuentes/disputa-de-apofis-y-seqenenre/so.texto: Papyrus copied by the scribe Pentawer under Merenptah (fragmentary)

fuentes/disputa-de-apofis-y-seqenenre/re.texto: A 19th Dynasty tale that sets the action at the end of the Second Intermediate Period, between the Hyksos Apophis and Seqenenre Tao, although the text is not historically accurate. From Avaris, Apophis challenges Seqenenre with a riddle: the hippopotamuses of Thebes disturb his sleep. The ending is lost.

fuentes/disputa-de-apofis-y-seqenenre/po.texto: It is a Ramesside tradition about the war against the Hyksos, not a document from the time it narrates.

fuentes/estela-de-la-tempestad/soporte.texto: Broken stela, found in the third pylon of Karnak between 1947 and 1951

fuentes/estela-de-la-tempestad/resumen.texto: Stela of Ahmose I describing a great storm over Egypt, which destroyed tombs, temples and pyramids in the Theban region, and the restoration that the king ordered. Vandersleyen published it in 1967 and 1968.

fuentes/estela-de-la-tempestad/por_que_i.texto: It has been linked to the eruption of Thera, a link that is disputed and depends on the date given to the eruption.

fuentes/estela-de-tombos/soporte.texto: Rock inscription on a granite boulder, on the east bank of the Nile, found around 1829

fuentes/estela-de-tombos/resumen.texto: Inscription of year 2 of Thutmose I that records his military campaign in Nubia, around the Third Cataract. It is part of a group of Egyptian inscriptions at Tombos, one of which celebrates the defeat of Kush.

fuentes/estela-de-tombos/por_que_importa.texto: It is the main text on Thutmose I's campaign in Kush and on the frontier of the empire at the Third Cataract.

fuentes/estela-de-tombos/leer.0.titulo.texto: Translation by Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 2 (1906)

fuentes/inscripcion-del-speos-artemidos/.texto: Inscription of the temple cut into the rock of Pakhet, near Beni Hasan

Text of the temple of Pakhet in which Hatshepsut denounces the Hyksos and tells how she repaired the damage they had caused, thereby legitimizing her reign. Brand holds that part of the temple's deterioration was caused by Thutmose III and repaired by Seti I.
It is one of the sources of Egyptian memory of the Hyksos a century after their expulsion.
Translation by Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 2 (1906)

fuentes/cuento-de-la-toma-de-jaffa/resum.texto: Tale of the conquest of the Canaanite city of Yapu (Joppa) by the general Djehuty, of Thutmose III. It is regarded as a purely literary account, but the excavators of Jaffa propose that a destruction of the Egyptian garrison, dated between 1456 and 1400 BC, was its historical basis.

fuentes/cuento-de-la-toma-de-jaffa/por_q.texto: It is a later literary tradition about an episode of the campaigns of Thutmose III, and the archaeology of Jaffa partly supports it.

fuentes/cuento-de-la-toma-de-jaffa/leer..texto: English translation on Wikisource (Egyptian Literature, “The Taking of Joppa”)

fuentes/papiro-medico-de-londres/resumen.texto: New Kingdom papyrus with 61 recipes, of which 25 are medical and the rest magical. It deals with skin and eye ailments and haemorrhages, above all with magic to prevent miscarriage.

fuentes/papiro-medico-de-londres/por_que.texto: It complements the Ebers and Edwin Smith papyri in the study of Egyptian medicine.

fuentes/letania-de-ra/resumen.texto: Important New Kingdom funerary text, reserved for pharaohs and highly favoured nobles, written inside the tomb. Its first part invokes the sun god Ra in 75 forms. It is known from the burial chamber of Thutmose III and the tomb of his vizier Useramun, and from the time of Seti I it was used at the entrance of most tombs.

fuentes/letania-de-ra/por_que_importa.texto: It shows the solar theology of New Kingdom royal tombs.

fuentes/gran-inscripcion-de-karnak/sopor.texto: Mural inscription of 79 lines, on the east wall of the courtyard of the cachette of the precinct of Amun-Ra

fuentes/gran-inscripcion-de-karnak/resum.texto: Long hieroglyphic inscription of Merenptah that includes the account of his campaigns against the Libyans and the Sea Peoples in the battle of Perire. It was discovered in 1828–1829; Champollion identified it and Lepsius published part of it.

fuentes/gran-inscripcion-de-karnak/por_q.texto: It is the most extensive source on Merenptah's war against the Libyans, together with his stela.

fuentes/gran-inscripcion-de-karnak/leer..texto: Breasted's translation, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 3 (1906)

fuentes/papiro-lansing/resumen.texto: Document of the 20th Dynasty put in the mouth of Nebmare-nakht, royal scribe and chief overseer of the cattle of Amun, and addressed to his pupil Wenemdiamun. It defends the advantages of being a scribe and disparages the other trades.

fuentes/papiro-lansing/por_que_importa.texto: It belongs to the genre of satires on trades, now with Ramesside society.

fuentes/papiro-brugsch/soporte.texto: Papyrus (Berlin Museum), found by Passalacqua at Saqqara

fuentes/papiro-brugsch/resumen.texto: Important medical papyrus whose writing dates from the 19th Dynasty, between 1350 and 1200 BC. Giuseppe Passalacqua found it at Saqqara, and Frederick William IV of Prussia acquired it for the Berlin Museum in 1827.

fuentes/papiro-brugsch/por_que_importa.texto: It is a source on New Kingdom medicine, together with the Ebers and Edwin Smith papyri.

fuentes/libro-de-las-puertas/soporte.texto: Scenes in royal tombs, from the 18th to the 20th Dynasties

fuentes/libro-de-las-puertas/resumen.texto: Long and detailed New Kingdom funerary text, with one hundred scenes, that narrates the passage of a newly dead soul into the otherworld with the sun god Ra through the underworld during the hours of the night. The oldest version, incomplete, is in the tomb of Horemheb; Seti I has the first complete one, on his sarcophagus.

fuentes/libro-de-las-puertas/por_que_imp.texto: It replaced the Amduat as the common funerary text of kings and shows the image of the underworld at the end of the 18th and in the 19th Dynasty.

fuentes/libro-de-las-cavernas/resumen.texto: New Kingdom underworld book, which originated in the 13th century BC, in the Ramesside period. Like the other underworld books, it is found in funerary contexts, tombs or temples, and describes the journey of the sun god Ra.

fuentes/libro-de-las-cavernas/por_que_im.texto: It is part of the corpus of New Kingdom underworld books.

fuentes/libro-de-la-tierra/resumen.texto: Egyptian funerary text also called The Creation of the Solar Disk and Book of Aker. It appears above all in the tombs of Merenptah, Tausret, Ramesses III, Ramesses VI and Ramesses VII.

fuentes/libro-de-la-tierra/por_que_impor.texto: It is part of the corpus of New Kingdom underworld books.

fuentes/canciones-del-arpista/soporte.texto: Tomb inscriptions of the Middle Kingdom and papyri up to Papyrus Harris 500

fuentes/canciones-del-arpista/resumen.texto: Egyptian texts that originated in Middle Kingdom tomb inscriptions and are found in papyri up to Papyrus Harris 500 of the New Kingdom. In general they praise life after death, although they show varying degrees of hope in it, and they were used in funerary contexts.

fuentes/canciones-del-arpista/por_que_im.texto: It shows attitudes toward death in Egyptian literature over several centuries.

fuentes/cuento-de-la-verdad-y-la-mentira.texto: The Blinding of Truth by Falsehood
Tale of the 19th Dynasty that recounts the dispute between Maat (Truth), her unnamed son and Gereg (Falsehood). It survives in Chester Beatty Papyrus II.
It is one of the New Kingdom tales with divine characters.

fuentes/mapa-del-papiro-de-turin/soporte.texto: Papyrus (Egyptian Museum, Turin), drawn on the recto

fuentes/mapa-del-papiro-de-turin/resumen.texto: Map on papyrus, also called the Mine Papyrus or Gold Mine Papyrus, dated to 1155–1150 BC and showing Wadi Hammamat in the eastern desert; the verso carries unrelated hieratic texts. It is linked to a quarrying expedition organized in year 3 of Ramesses IV to obtain blocks of bekhen stone.

fuentes/mapa-del-papiro-de-turin/por_que.texto: It is considered one of the oldest known geographical maps and the oldest surviving topographical map of Egypt.

fuentes/onomastico-de-amenope/soporte.texto: Papyrus found at el-Hiba, from the Golenishchev collection

fuentes/onomastico-de-amenope/resumen.texto: Egyptian text dated from the end of the 20th Dynasty to the 22nd Dynasty. It is a compilation of a tradition that began in the Middle Kingdom and that includes the Ramesseum Onomasticon, from the end of the 20th Dynasty.

fuentes/onomastico-de-amenope/por_que_im.texto: It is a list of names of the Egyptian world, from gods to places, used as a school and reference text.

fuentes/cuento-del-infortunio/soporte.texto: Papyrus Moscow 127, from the Golenishchev collection

fuentes/cuento-del-infortunio/resumen.texto: Egyptian document from the end of the 20th Dynasty to the 22nd Dynasty, part of a collection of three papyri with the Onomasticon of Amenope and the Report of Wenamun, discovered at el-Hiba. It is also called the Letter of Wermai.

fuentes/cuento-del-infortunio/por_que_im.texto: It is a source on the literature and administration of the Renaissance era.

fuentes/papiro-erotico-de-turin/soporte.texto: Painted papyrus roll (Egyptian Museum, Turin, papyrus 55001)

fuentes/papiro-erotico-de-turin/resumen.texto: Painted papyrus of the Ramesside period, c. 1150 BC, discovered at Deir el-Medina at the beginning of the 19th century.

fuentes/papiro-erotico-de-turin/por_que_.texto: It is one of the few surviving Egyptian representations of sexuality, and it is studied for its style and its possible function.

fuentes/papiro-medico-chester-beatty/sop.texto: Papyrus from the Alfred Chester Beatty collection

fuentes/papiro-medico-chester-beatty/res.texto: Medical papyrus dated to c. 1200 BC, which contains magic spells against headaches and remedies for anorectal ailments.

fuentes/papiro-medico-chester-beatty/por.texto: It is a source on Egyptian medicine of the 19th Dynasty.

personas/mentuhotep-ii/resumen.texto: King of the 11th Dynasty who reigned c. 2055–2004 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). He reunified Egypt after subduing the rulers of Herakleopolis, probably shortly before his year 39 of reign, and was buried in his funerary temple at Deir el-Bahari, in Thebes.

personas/mentuhotep-iii/resumen.texto: King of the 11th Dynasty who reigned c. 2004–1992 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). He is credited with reopening the Punt route through the Red Sea, which is documented by an inscription of his official Henenu in Wadi Hammamat.

personas/mentuhotep-iv/resumen.texto: Last king of the 11th Dynasty, who reigned c. 1992–1985 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). He is missing from the Abydos King List and the Turin Canon, and is known from inscriptions in Wadi Hammamat, where his vizier Amenemhat appears, whom some Egyptologists identify with the future Amenemhat I.

personas/amenemhat-i/resumen.texto: Founder of the 12th Dynasty, who reigned c. 1985–1956 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000) and moved the capital to Itjtawy. The Instruction of Amenemhat and the Story of Sinuhe show him dead in a palace plot, a literary account with no other confirmation.

personas/sesostris-i/resumen.texto: King of the 12th Dynasty who reigned c. 1956–1911 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), with a coregency with his father whose existence is disputed. He had the White Chapel of Karnak built, an obelisk at Heliopolis and his pyramid at el-Lisht, and he extended the Egyptian frontier in Nubia as far as Buhen.

personas/amenemhat-ii/resumen.texto: King of the 12th Dynasty who reigned c. 1911–1877 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). His Annals, found at Memphis, record expeditions to Lebanon, to Asia (the destruction of Iuai and Iasy) and to Sinai, and he was buried in a pyramid at Dahshur.

personas/sesostris-ii/resumen.texto: King of the 12th Dynasty who reigned c. 1877–1870 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). He built his pyramid at Lahun, at the entrance to the Fayum, next to the workers' town now called Kahun.

personas/sesostris-iii/resumen.texto: King of the 12th Dynasty who reigned c. 1870–1831 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). He pushed the southern frontier to Semna with campaigns in Nubia and a chain of fortresses, and he is credited with a reduction in the power of the nomarchs.

personas/amenemhat-iii/resumen.texto: King of the 12th Dynasty who reigned c. 1831–1786 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), for about forty-five years. He promoted the water works of the Fayum, exploited the turquoise mines of Sinai and was buried in a pyramid at Hawara.

personas/amenemhat-iv/resumen.texto: King of the 12th Dynasty who reigned c. 1786–1777 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), for about nine years. Little survives of his reign, which is mentioned by inscriptions from Sinai and Nubia.

personas/sobekneferu/resumen.texto: Last ruler of the 12th Dynasty, who reigned c. 1777–1773 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), about four years according to the Turin Canon. She is the first woman known to have held the full royal titulary in Egypt.

personas/sobekhotep-i/resumen.texto: King of the 13th Dynasty whom Kim Ryholt (1997) makes the founder, with three or four years of reign around 1803–1800 BC; the hypothesis is now dominant, but his place in the list is disputed. Ryholt makes the dynasty last from 1803 to 1649 BC, and Shaw makes it begin c. 1773.

personas/amenemhat-v/resumen.texto: King of the 13th Dynasty, fourth in the list according to Ryholt and Baker, who make him reign c. 1796–1793 BC. Some Egyptologists identify him with Sekhemkare Amenemhat Senebef, and others regard him as a different king.

personas/ameny-qemau/resumen.texto: King of the 13th Dynasty who, according to Ryholt and Baker, reigned two years, c. 1793–1791 BC. His pyramid at Dahshur South, with a burial chamber cut from a single block of quartzite and fragments of canopic jars bearing his name, is one of the few royal tombs of that dynasty; Musès found it in 1957.

personas/sobekhotep-iii/resumen.texto: King of the middle of the 13th Dynasty who reigned four years. His chronology is approximate (according to Ryholt, 1997), and he is placed in the middle of the 18th century BC.

personas/neferhotep-i/resumen.texto: King of the 13th Dynasty who reigned eleven years according to the Turin Canon, c. 1740–1730 BC, with approximate chronology (Ryholt dates the start of his reign to c. 1740 BC). He is one of the best-attested kings of that dynasty, with monuments from Byblos to Nubia, and he was succeeded by his brother Sobekhotep IV.

personas/sobekhotep-iv/resumen.texto: King of the 13th Dynasty who reigned about ten years in the middle of the 18th century BC (approximate chronology, according to Ryholt), and one of the best attested of that dynasty. Brother of Neferhotep I, he was born in Thebes according to a stela from Karnak.

personas/khendjer/resumen.texto: King of the 13th Dynasty who reigned about three to five years, c. 1764–1759 BC according to Ryholt and Baker. He had a small pyramid built at Saqqara South, from which it is supposed that he governed from Memphis.

personas/merneferre-ay/resumen.texto: The king of the 13th Dynasty with the longest reign, more than twenty-three years, who according to Ryholt ruled c. 1701–1677 BC (Schneider places him in 1684–1661). He is the last of his dynasty attested outside Upper Egypt.

personas/nehesy/resumen.texto: Ruler of Lower Egypt from Avaris, placed by most Egyptologists in the 14th Dynasty around 1705 BC. According to Ryholt he was the son of Sheshi and of a queen Tati, and many objects attributed to him could belong to a Hyksos prince of the same name, c. 1580 BC.

personas/yakbim/resumen.texto: Ruler of the Second Intermediate Period with a Semitic name, whom Ryholt regards as the founder of the 14th Dynasty, of Levantine descent, with about twenty-five years of reign c. 1805–1780 BC. In older literature he was placed in the 16th Dynasty.

personas/sheshi/resumen.texto: Ruler of the Second Intermediate Period known from many seals, more than any other from the period between the Middle Kingdom and the Hyksos. His dynasty, his chronology and the extent of his domain are disputed.

personas/salitis/resumen.texto: Name by which Josephus, citing Manetho, calls the first Hyksos king; he cannot be securely identified with any king in the inscriptions. The 15th Dynasty ruled c. 1650–1550 BC from Avaris.

personas/khyan/resumen.texto: Hyksos king of the 15th Dynasty, in the second half of the 17th century BC. Objects bearing his name have been found at Knossos and Hattusa, and a sphinx of his was bought in the Baghdad market, which shows the extent of his contacts.

personas/apepi/resumen.texto: Hyksos king of the 15th Dynasty who reigned about forty years until the middle of the 16th century BC. According to the Carnarvon Tablet and the stela of Kamose, he was the king against whom the rulers of Thebes fought.

personas/khamudi/resumen.texto: Last king of the 15th Dynasty, who reigned c. 1550 BC. He was the Hyksos king in Avaris when Ahmose I took the city, although the tradition is not unanimous about how the dynasty ended.

personas/senebkay/resumen.texto: King of the Abydos Dynasty, discovered in 2014 through his tomb at Abydos, whose inscriptions name him as king. His discovery supports the existence of an independent kingdom in Upper Egypt, contemporary with the 15th and 16th Dynasties.

personas/rahotep/resumen.texto: Theban king of the Second Intermediate Period. Ryholt and Baker regard him as the first king of the 17th Dynasty, around 1580 BC, and Rahotep restored temples at Abydos and Koptos.

personas/sobekemsaf-ii/resumen.texto: Theban king of the 17th Dynasty during the Second Intermediate Period. His tomb at Dra Abu el-Naga was robbed, and the theft appears in the Abbott Papyrus, which records the inspection, and in the Leopold II–Amherst Papyrus, with the confessions of the thieves.

personas/nubkheperre-intef/resumen.texto: King of the 17th Dynasty at Thebes, c. 1560 BC, the best attested of Seqenenre's predecessors. His coffin and monuments come from Dra Abu el-Naga.

personas/seqenenre-tao/resumen.texto: Theban king of the 17th Dynasty, father of Ahmose I and probably of Kamose, although other authors make Kamose his brother. His mummy shows head wounds compatible with a violent death, which is associated with the war against the Hyksos without direct proof.

personas/kamose/resumen.texto: Last king of the 17th Dynasty, whom Ryholt makes reign c. 1554–1549 BC. His two stelae from Karnak narrate his advance against Apepi and the Hyksos and the interception of a messenger of Apepi to the ruler of Kush.

personas/ahmose-sitkamose/resumen.texto: Only known daughter of Kamose, married to her uncle Ahmose I, Great Royal Wife and God's Wife. Her mummy appeared in 1881 in the cache of Deir el-Bahari (DB320).

personas/ahmose-i/resumen.texto: Founder of the 18th Dynasty, who reigned c. 1550–1525 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). He ended the war against the Hyksos with the capture of Avaris and Sharuhen and reopened the frontier with Nubia.

personas/amenhotep-i/resumen.texto: King of the 18th Dynasty who reigned c. 1525–1504 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). He campaigned in Nubia and, after his death, was venerated together with his mother Ahmose-Nefertari as patron of the village of Deir el-Medina.

personas/tutmosis-i/resumen.texto: King of the 18th Dynasty who reigned c. 1504–1492 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000) and took Egyptian campaigns as far as the Euphrates and the Third Cataract. He is credited with the first royal tomb in the Valley of the Kings, an attribution disputed between KV20 and KV38.

personas/tutmosis-ii/resumen.texto: King of the 18th Dynasty who reigned c. 1492–1479 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), married to his half-sister Hatshepsut. His inscriptions record a campaign in Nubia, and the autobiography of Ahmose Pennekhbet recounts an action against the Shasu. His tomb was found in 2025 in Wadi C-4.

personas/amenhotep-ii/resumen.texto: King of the 18th Dynasty who reigned c. 1427–1400 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). He campaigned in Syria and Palestine, and his tomb in the Valley of the Kings (KV35) later held a cache of royal mummies.

personas/tutmosis-iv/resumen.texto: King of the 18th Dynasty who reigned c. 1400–1390 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). The Dream Stela, between the paws of the Great Sphinx of Giza, presents him as chosen for the throne; he married a princess of Mitanni.

personas/amenhotep-iii/resumen.texto: King of the 18th Dynasty who reigned c. 1390–1352 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), of whom about two hundred and fifty statues survive. His reign coincides with the beginning of the diplomatic correspondence of the Amarna Letters and with the buildings at Luxor, Soleb and the palace of Malkata.

personas/semenejkara/resumen.texto: Coregent or brief successor of Akhenaten, c. 1338–1336 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). His identity is disputed: he has been regarded as a son of Amenhotep III, as Nefertiti under another name, or as a different king.

personas/neferneferuaten/resumen.texto: Name of a ruler from the late Amarna period, with a feminine epithet in some inscriptions. His chronology is very uncertain, and Shaw's table gives him no dates of his own. Some Egyptologists identify him with Nefertiti and others with Meritaten.

personas/tutankamon/resumen.texto: King of the 18th Dynasty who reigned c. 1336–1327 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), a child when he came to the throne. He reversed the Amarna religious policy with the Restoration Stela, and his tomb, found almost intact in 1922 (it had been robbed in antiquity), is the best preserved in the Valley of the Kings.

personas/ay/resumen.texto: King of the 18th Dynasty who reigned c. 1327–1323 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). He had been a high official under Akhenaten and Tutankhamun, and in the paintings of Tutankhamun's tomb he officiates at the Opening of the Mouth ritual.

personas/horemheb/resumen.texto: General under Tutankhamun and last king of the 18th Dynasty, who reigned c. 1323–1295 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). His edict reorganized the administration, and his tombs, one at Saqqara and another in the Valley of the Kings, survive.

personas/ramses-i/resumen.texto: First king of the 19th Dynasty, who reigned c. 1295–1294 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), barely more than a year. He was a soldier of non-royal origin and the heir designated by Horemheb.

personas/seti-i/resumen.texto: King of the 19th Dynasty who reigned c. 1294–1279 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), father of Ramesses II. He campaigned in Syria and against Libya, built the hypostyle hall of Karnak and his temple at Abydos, with the Abydos King List.

personas/merenptah/resumen.texto: King of the 19th Dynasty who reigned c. 1213–1203 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), the thirteenth son of Ramesses II. He defeated the Libyans and their allies in the Delta in year 5, and his Merneptah Stela contains the earliest mention of Israel that is generally accepted.

personas/amenmeses/resumen.texto: King of the 19th Dynasty who reigned c. 1203–1200 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), with a dominion perhaps limited to Thebes and Nubia. His relationship with Seti II is disputed: he has been regarded as a usurper or as a rival in a civil war.

personas/seti-ii/resumen.texto: King of the 19th Dynasty who reigned c. 1200–1194 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). He had to face a rival, Amenmesse, who according to one theory took Thebes and Nubia, and his tomb KV15 has royal names deliberately erased.

personas/siptah/resumen.texto: King of the 19th Dynasty who reigned c. 1194–1188 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), a child when he came to the throne. He ruled under the guardianship of Tausert and the chancellor Bay, and his mummy shows a deformity of the left foot.

personas/tausert/resumen.texto: Wife of Seti II and king of the 19th Dynasty in her own right, c. 1188–1186 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). She was the last ruler of the dynasty, and her tomb, KV14, was reused by Setnakht.

personas/setnajt/resumen.texto: Founder of the 20th Dynasty, who reigned c. 1186–1184 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). His Elephantine Stela says that he restored order after a period of disorder and the presence of foreigners in the country.

personas/ramses-iii/resumen.texto: King of the 20th Dynasty who reigned c. 1184–1153 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). He repelled the Libyans and the Sea Peoples, built Medinet Habu, and died after the harem conspiracy, which was investigated in a trial documented in the Turin Judicial Papyrus.

personas/ramses-iv/resumen.texto: King of the 20th Dynasty who reigned c. 1153–1147 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), son of Ramesses III. Under his reign the Harris I Papyrus, which lists the works of his father, was written, and the scribe Amennakhte drew the Turin Papyrus Map for an expedition to Wadi Hammamat.

personas/ramses-v/resumen.texto: King of the 20th Dynasty who reigned c. 1147–1143 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). His mummy shows skin lesions that have been interpreted as smallpox, without a certain diagnosis.

personas/ramses-vi/resumen.texto: King of the 20th Dynasty who reigned c. 1143–1136 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), son of Ramesses III and Iset Ta-Hemdjert. He took over the tomb KV9 in the Valley of the Kings, which had been planned for Ramesses V, and enlarged and redecorated it.

personas/ramses-vii/resumen.texto: King of the 20th Dynasty who reigned c. 1136–1129 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), son of Ramesses VI. His reign is poorly documented.

personas/ramses-viii/resumen.texto: King of the 20th Dynasty who reigned c. 1129–1126 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), for a year at most, a figure deduced from the few attestations that mention him. Son of Ramesses III, he is barely documented.

personas/ramses-ix/resumen.texto: King of the 20th Dynasty who reigned c. 1126–1108 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). Under his reign took place the investigation of the robberies of royal tombs at Thebes recorded in the Abbott Papyrus and the Amherst Papyrus.

personas/ramses-x/resumen.texto: King of the 20th Dynasty who reigned c. 1108–1099 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). His tomb in the Valley of the Kings, KV18, was left unfinished.

personas/ramses-xi/resumen.texto: Last king of the 20th Dynasty and of the New Kingdom, who reigned c. 1099–1069 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). His power in Upper Egypt passed to Herihor, High Priest of Amun, and other military men during the so-called “Renaissance era”.

personas/ahhotep-i/resumen.texto: Queen of the 17th Dynasty, daughter of Senakhtenre and Tetisheri, wife of Seqenenre, mother of Ahmose I and probable regent for her son. A stela from Karnak praises her role in the kingdom, although her part in the war against the Hyksos is a hypothesis of Egyptologists; a coffin from the Deir el-Bahari cache is attributed to her.

personas/ahmose-nefertari/resumen.texto: Wife of Ahmose I and mother of Amenhotep I, the first to hold the title God's Wife of Amun. After her death she was venerated, together with her son, as patron of the Theban necropolis.

personas/tetisheri/resumen.texto: Queen of the 17th Dynasty, wife of Senakhtenre Ahmose and grandmother of Ahmose I. Her chapel at Abydos was erected by her grandson and is the main source on her.

personas/ahhotep-ii/resumen.texto: Queen of the late 17th Dynasty, probably Great Royal Wife of Kamose. Her coffin, found at Dra Abu el-Naga in 1859, contained a treasure of jewelry with the names of Kamose and Ahmose I.

personas/ahmose-meritamun/resumen.texto: Queen at the beginning of the 18th Dynasty, elder sister and wife of Amenhotep I. She died young and was buried in tomb TT358 at Deir el-Bahari.

personas/mutnofret/resumen.texto: Queen of the 18th Dynasty, secondary wife of Thutmose I and mother of his successor Thutmose II. From her title King's Daughter she is supposed to have been a daughter of Ahmose I and sister of Amenhotep I.

personas/neferura/resumen.texto: Daughter of Hatshepsut and Thutmose II, with the title God's Wife. She appears with Senenmut, her tutor, in several statues; her last mention is a stela from Serabit el-Khadim of year 11 of Thutmose III, which does not name the king, and she is absent from Senenmut's second tomb, so she may have died during her mother's reign.

personas/meritra-hatshepsut/resumen.texto: Wife of Thutmose III and mother of Amenhotep II, who served as Great Royal Wife. Her planned tomb was KV42, and perhaps she was buried in KV35; she is known from KV34, TT72 and statues.

personas/mutemuia/resumen.texto: Wife of Thutmose IV and mother of Amenhotep III, whom he had represented in the temple of Luxor. Her origin is disputed, and she has been assumed to be from Mitanni, without evidence.

personas/tiy/resumen.texto: Great Royal Wife of Amenhotep III and mother of Akhenaten, daughter of Yuya and Tuya. The Amarna Letters show her influence on diplomacy, and her figure appears next to the Aten.

personas/yuya/resumen.texto: Courtier of the 18th Dynasty and father of Queen Tiye, married to Tuya. His almost intact tomb in the Valley of the Kings (KV46), found in 1905, contains his mummy and that of his wife.

personas/tuya/resumen.texto: Egyptian noblewoman, wife of Yuya, mother of Queen Tiye and grandmother of Akhenaten. She was buried with her husband in tomb KV46 in the Valley of the Kings.

personas/sitamon/resumen.texto: Eldest daughter of Amenhotep III and Tiye, whom her father took as a wife. She had her own properties, and she is mentioned in objects from the palace of Malkata.

personas/gilukhepa/resumen.texto: Princess of Mitanni, sister of Tushratta, who came to Egypt in year 10 of Amenhotep III to marry him. A commemorative scarab of Amenhotep III records her arrival with an entourage of more than three hundred women.

personas/tadukhepa/resumen.texto: Princess of Mitanni, daughter of Tushratta, sent to Egypt to marry Amenhotep III, and who later passed, according to the Amarna Letters, into the harem of Akhenaten. It is disputed whether she is the Kiya of the Amarna inscriptions.

personas/kiya/resumen.texto: Minor wife of Akhenaten, with the title Beloved Wife, whose monuments were rewritten after she disappeared from the records. It is disputed whether she was the mother of Tutankhamun and whether she was the Mitannian princess Tadukhepa.

personas/meritaton/resumen.texto: Eldest daughter of Akhenaten and Nefertiti, Great Royal Wife of Smenkhkare. Some Egyptologists identify her with Neferneferuaten, who reigned briefly.

personas/meketaton/resumen.texto: Second daughter of Akhenaten and Nefertiti, who died young at Amarna. The mourning scenes in the royal tomb at Amarna (TA26) are associated with her.

personas/anjesenamon/resumen.texto: Daughter of Akhenaten and Nefertiti and wife of Tutankhamun, whose original name was Ankhesenpaaten. After the death of her husband, according to a Hittite letter, an Egyptian queen asked Suppiluliuma I for a son as her husband, an event that tradition attributes to her without certainty.

personas/beketaton/resumen.texto: Princess of the 18th Dynasty, considered the youngest daughter of Amenhotep III and Tiye and therefore sister of Akhenaten. Her name means “servant of the Aten”.

personas/nefertari/resumen.texto: Great Royal Wife of Ramesses II, for whom the smaller temple at Abu Simbel was built. Her tomb, QV66 in the Valley of the Queens, is famous for its paintings.

personas/isetnofret/resumen.texto: Great Royal Wife of Ramesses II and mother of Khaemwaset and Merneptah. She became the chief queen after the death of Nefertari.

personas/bintanat/resumen.texto: Daughter of Ramesses II and Isetnofret, who was his Great Royal Wife. She appears in a colossal statue at Akhmim, and she is mentioned as the eldest daughter.

personas/meritamon/resumen.texto: Daughter of Ramesses II and Nefertari, who was his Great Royal Wife and had a colossal statue at Akhmim. Her tomb is in the Valley of the Queens (QV68).

personas/henutmira/resumen.texto: Princess and queen of the 19th Dynasty, one of the eight Great Royal Wives of Ramesses II. A statue calls her the king's daughter of his body and Great Royal Wife: she was a daughter of Ramesses II, and the idea that she was his sister comes from a statue of Tuya.

personas/amenherjepeshef/resumen.texto: First son of Ramesses II and his heir, whose military titles reflect that status and who appears in war scenes. He died around year 25 of his father's reign, before him, so Ramesses II designated other heirs.

personas/jaemuaset/resumen.texto: Fourth son of Ramesses II, High Priest of Ptah at Memphis, who directed the burial of Apis bulls in the Serapeum of Saqqara and restored pyramids and other monuments of the Old Kingdom. He died around year 55 of his father's reign, after which Merneptah was proclaimed heir.

personas/tiy-merenese/resumen.texto: Great Royal Wife of Setnakht and mother of Ramesses III. She is known from a stela from Abydos and from blocks reused on the same site.

personas/iset-ta-hemdjert/resumen.texto: Wife of Ramesses III and mother of Ramesses VI, whom she bore as Great Royal Wife. She was buried in QV51 and was probably of Asiatic origin, since her mother had a Syrian name.

personas/pentaur-principe/resumen.texto: Prince of the 20th Dynasty, son of Ramesses III and of Tiye, a secondary wife of the king, whom the Turin Judicial Papyrus mentions among those condemned for the harem conspiracy and who was forced to take his own life. He has been proposed as the identity of the mummy called “Unknown Man E”; a 2012 DNA study showed that “Unknown Man E” is a son of Ramesses III, which supports the identification, although nothing proves the name.

personas/sobekemsaf-i/resumen.texto: King of the 17th Dynasty during the Second Intermediate Period, predecessor of Nubkheperre Intef. He is placed shortly before Sobekemsaf II, after whom the Intef kings succeed.

personas/ineni/resumen.texto: Architect and official of the 18th Dynasty who served under Amenhotep I, Thutmose I and II, and Hatshepsut. He directed works at Karnak and, probably, the first tomb in the Valley of the Kings.

personas/ahmose-hijo-de-ebana/resumen.texto: Soldier from Elkab who served Ahmose I, Amenhotep I and Thutmose I; his autobiography in the tomb at Elkab is the main source on the war against the Hyksos and on the campaigns in Nubia and Syria. He should not be confused with King Ahmose I.

personas/ahmose-pennejbet/resumen.texto: Military man from El Kab who began to serve under Ahmose I and continued with all the kings up to Thutmose III. His autobiography, in his tomb (EK2), recounts campaigns with Ahmose I in northern Canaan, with Amenhotep I in Nubia, with Thutmose I in Naharin and with Thutmose II in Sinai; he was also tutor of Neferura.

personas/senenmut/resumen.texto: High official of Hatshepsut, steward of Amun and tutor of her daughter Neferura, with probable involvement in the temple of Deir el-Bahari. His name was later erased from several monuments, and his end is not known with certainty.

personas/hapuseneb/resumen.texto: High priest of Amun during the reign of Hatshepsut. He is known from his Theban tomb and from statues of the period.

personas/rejmira/resumen.texto: Governor of Thebes and vizier under Thutmose III and Amenhotep II. His Theban tomb TT100, in Sheikh Abd el-Qurna, has scenes of tribute and craftsmen.

personas/amenhotep-hijo-de-hapu/resumen.texto: Official and architect of Amenhotep III, who directed works such as his funerary temple in West Thebes, of which the Colossi of Memnon remain. After his death he was venerated as a sage.

personas/nakhtmin/resumen.texto: General during the reign of Tutankhamun, who was heir to the throne under Ay without ever reigning. Ushabtis bearing his name were found in the tomb of Tutankhamun.

personas/maya-tesorero/resumen.texto: Supervisor of the treasuries under Tutankhamun, Ay and Horemheb, alive at least until year 8 of Horemheb, when he was put in charge of tax collection.

personas/usersatet/resumen.texto: Viceroy of Kush under Amenhotep II and perhaps in the first years of Thutmose IV. He followed the king on his Syrian campaign, cleared five canals at Aswan and left many monuments in Lower Nubia.

personas/merimose/resumen.texto: Viceroy of Kush during almost the whole reign of Amenhotep III. He led a campaign in Nubia, in which the death of 312 Nubians and the capture of 740 prisoners are recorded.

personas/nehi/resumen.texto: Viceroy of Kush under Thutmose III, whom he accompanied on the Syrian campaign of year 23. He left inscriptions at several sites in Nubia and was buried in Thebes.

personas/paser-visir/resumen.texto: Vizier of Seti I and of the early reign of Ramesses II, whose tomb (TT106) in Thebes survives. He later became high priest of Amun.

personas/ramose/resumen.texto: Vizier of Amenhotep III and Akhenaten, whose Theban tomb (TT55) has reliefs from the transition to Amarna. He is known for his double style, traditional and Atenist.

personas/pareherwenemef/resumen.texto: Prince of the 19th Dynasty, third son of Ramesses II and second of Nefertari. He appears in the Kadesh scenes of his father's temples.

personas/bay-canciller/resumen.texto: Official of Asiatic origin who reached the office of chancellor under Seti II and was a figure of power at the end of the 19th Dynasty. His identification with the Syrian Irsu of Papyrus Harris is disputed. An ostracon records that King Siptah ordered his execution around his year 5.

personas/herihor/resumen.texto: Army officer, vizier and finally ruler of Upper Egypt as high priest of Amun at Thebes, c. 1080–1074 BC, during the reign of Ramesses XI. His figure marks the beginning of the division of Egypt between Thebes and the Delta.

personas/pinedjem-i/resumen.texto: High priest of Amun, son of Piankh, who already in the Third Intermediate Period assumed royal titulary at Thebes. He appears here only as the close of the New Kingdom, because of his role as successor of Herihor.

personas/paneb/resumen.texto: Foreman of the work gang of Deir el-Medina under Seti II, whom the Salt Papyrus 124 accuses of theft, violence and abuse. The document, from the period, is an accusation and not the sentence, which is not preserved.

personas/rib-hadda/resumen.texto: Ruler of Byblos and author of dozens of letters to the pharaoh in the Amarna archive, the longest series from a single sender. He asks for help against Abdi-Ashirta and his son Aziru, and was finally displaced.

personas/abdi-heba/resumen.texto: Ruler of Jerusalem in the Amarna Letters, who maintains in his letters that he was appointed by the king and did not inherit the office. His writings denounce other Canaanite rulers.

personas/labaya/resumen.texto: Ruler of Shechem in the Amarna letters, accused by other rulers of expanding and of rebelling against the pharaoh. According to those letters, he died at the hands of other rulers.

personas/aziru/resumen.texto: King of Amurru, son of Abdi-Ashirta, and author of letters to Akhenaten; he was summoned to Egypt and held there, and on his return he went over to the Hittite side, with a treaty with Suppiluliuma I. His correspondence with Rib-Hadda and his rivals shows Amurru's shift toward the Hittites.

personas/jnumhotep-ii/resumen.texto: Nomarch of the Oryx nome (16th of Upper Egypt), at Beni Hasan, under Amenemhat II and Senusret II. His tomb preserves a scene of a group of Asiatics arriving in Egypt and a long autobiography.

personas/djehutihotep/resumen.texto: Nomarch of the Hare nome, at Deir el-Bersha, around 1900 BC, under Amenemhat II, Senusret II and III. His tomb contains the scene of the transport of a colossal statue on a sledge.

personas/mutnedjmet/resumen.texto: Great Royal Wife of Horemheb, his second wife after Amenia, who died before he became king. She is the last queen of the 18th Dynasty.

personas/sitre/resumen.texto: Great Royal Wife of Ramesses I and mother of Seti I.

personas/tutmosis-principe/resumen.texto: Eldest son and first heir of Amenhotep III and Tiye, elder brother of the future Akhenaten. He died without reigning, and his younger brother became the heir.

personas/tutmose-escultor/resumen.texto: Sculptor of Akhenaten's court in the Amarna style, around 1345 BC. His workshop at Amarna, found by a German expedition, is where the bust of Nefertiti was found.

personas/meryra/resumen.texto: The only certain high priest of the Aten, with a tomb at Amarna (tomb 4). It is disputed whether he is the same official who appears in a tomb at Memphis under the name Meryneith.

personas/parennefer/resumen.texto: Counsellor of Akhenaten before he came to the throne, and later his royal cupbearer, with the titles of chief of craftsmen and supervisor of the works of the Mansion of the Aten.

personas/pentu/resumen.texto: Vizier under Tutankhamun, known only from a wine jar label found in the tomb of Tutankhamun. It has been proposed to identify him with Akhenaten's chief physician of the same name, a hypothesis not proven.

personas/ramessesnakht/resumen.texto: High priest of Amun at Thebes, appointed under Ramesses IV and in office until Ramesses IX. During his tenure the power of the priesthood of Amun grew while that of the pharaoh declined.

personas/amenhotep-sumo-sacerdote/resume.texto: High priest of Amun at the end of the 20th Dynasty, under Ramesses IX, X and XI, and son of Ramessesnakht. It is not known for certain whether Herihor succeeded him or whether there was another high priest between them.

personas/ahmose-sapair/resumen.texto: Prince of the late 17th Dynasty, son of Seqenenre Tao or of Kamose and brother of Ahmose I.

personas/wegaf/resumen.texto: King of the 13th Dynasty known from a stela and statues. The Turin Canon gives him as first king, with two years of reign, but according to Ryholt the scribe confused Khutawyre with Sekhemre Khutawy (Sobekhotep I), and Wegaf goes to the middle of the dynasty.

personas/amenemhat-vi/resumen.texto: King of the 13th Dynasty with a brief reign, of about three years or less, which Ryholt places c. 1788–1785 BC. He appears in two royal lists and on a few objects of his time.

personas/sewadjkare-hori/resumen.texto: King of the late 13th Dynasty, possibly the thirty-sixth of the dynasty. He reigned five years over Middle Egypt and Upper Egypt, in the middle of the 17th century BC.

personas/ibiau/resumen.texto: Minor king of the 13th Dynasty, perhaps with a reign of about ten years according to the Turin Canon.

personas/neferu-ii/resumen.texto: Wife and sister of Mentuhotep II, king of the 11th Dynasty, around 2050 BC.

personas/tem-reina/resumen.texto: Consort queen of the 11th Dynasty, wife of Mentuhotep II and mother of Mentuhotep III. She was buried in tomb DBXI.15 in her husband's funerary complex at Deir el-Bahari, during the reign of her son; she was probably of common origin.

personas/kawit/resumen.texto: Secondary wife of Mentuhotep II, buried in tomb DBXI.9 of the king's funerary temple at Deir el-Bahari, with a small decorated chapel. Several of the women buried there were priestesses of Hathor.

personas/kemsit/resumen.texto: Wife of Mentuhotep II of the 11th Dynasty. Her tomb (TT308) and a small decorated chapel were found behind the king's funerary temple at Deir el-Bahari, next to those of five other women.

personas/ashayet/resumen.texto: Wife of Mentuhotep II of the 11th Dynasty. Her tomb (DBXI.17) and a small decorated chapel were found in the king's funerary complex at Deir el-Bahari, with those of four other women of about twenty years of age and a girl.

personas/henhenet/resumen.texto: Lower-ranking wife of Mentuhotep II, of the 11th Dynasty. Her tomb (DBXI.11) and her decorated chapel were found behind the king's funerary temple at Deir el-Bahari.

personas/sadeh/resumen.texto: Lower-ranking wife of Mentuhotep II, of the 11th Dynasty, buried with other women in the king's funerary complex at Deir el-Bahari.

personas/dagi/resumen.texto: Vizier of Mentuhotep II known for his Theban tomb TT103, of which fragments of reliefs and traces of paintings survive, and for his decorated sarcophagus, now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

personas/meketre/resumen.texto: Chancellor and steward under Mentuhotep II and Mentuhotep III, and perhaps under Amenemhat I. He is famous for the models in his tomb TT280.

personas/ipi-visir/resumen.texto: Vizier at the beginning of the Middle Kingdom, in whose funerary complex at Deir el-Bahari the letters of Heqanakht, his ka-priest, were found.

personas/tia-princesa/resumen.texto: Daughter of Seti I and Tuya and elder sister of Ramesses II, married to an official also named Tia, outside the royal family. She is attested only in monuments of her brother's reign, and she is shown with her family in a tomb at Saqqara.

personas/ikhernofret/resumen.texto: Treasurer of the 12th Dynasty under Senusret III and into the first years of Amenemhat III, with the titles of supervisor of the double treasury and of the double Gold Palace and royal sealer. He is known from several stelae from Abydos, one with his biography (Berlin 1204).

personas/jnumhotep-i/resumen.texto: Great chief of the Oryx nome (16th of Upper Egypt) under Amenemhat I, of the 12th Dynasty, at the beginning of the 20th century BC.

personas/amenemhat-nomarca-del-orice/res.texto: Lord of the Oryx nome (16th of Upper Egypt) and high priest under Senusret I, of the 12th Dynasty, also called Ameny.

personas/jnumhotep-iii/resumen.texto: Greatest steward and vizier of the 12th Dynasty, son of the local ruler Khnumhotep II. Under Senusret II he was sent on several missions, to the Red Sea and to Byblos, and under Senusret III he built his mastaba at Dahshur and became vizier.

personas/sarenput-i/resumen.texto: Nomarch of Elephantine under Senusret I, of the 12th Dynasty.

personas/sarenput-ii/resumen.texto: Nomarch of Elephantine under Senusret II and Senusret III, also called Nubkaurenakht.

personas/intefiqer/resumen.texto: Vizier and city supervisor under Amenemhat I and his son Senusret I, at the beginning of the 12th Dynasty.

personas/sobekemhat/resumen.texto: Treasurer of Senusret III, known only from his mastaba, excavated in 1894 next to the king's pyramid at Dahshur, from which fragments of reliefs bearing his name and titles were found.

personas/siese/resumen.texto: Vizier and treasurer of the 12th Dynasty, probably under Senusret III. He began as chamberlain, became greatest steward and then treasurer; his mastaba at Dahshur was excavated by de Morgan around 1894–1895.

personas/iymeru/resumen.texto: Vizier of the 13th Dynasty, son of the vizier Ankhu and brother of Resseneb. According to Grajetzki, both held the office for a short time, and other sources place him under Khendjer and his successor Imyremeshaw, or later.

personas/neferu-iii/resumen.texto: Queen of the 12th Dynasty, daughter of Amenemhat I, sister and wife of Senusret I and mother of Amenemhat II.

personas/khenemetneferhedjet-i/resumen.texto: Queen of the 12th Dynasty, wife of Senusret II and mother of Senusret III. She is probably the daughter of Amenemhat II named on a seal, or else the sister of her husband.

personas/khenemetneferhedjet-ii/resumen.texto: Queen of the 12th Dynasty, one of the three known wives of Senusret III, with Neferthenut and Itakayt. Two statues of her husband mention her.

personas/sithathoriunet/resumen.texto: Daughter of the king of the 12th Dynasty, possibly of Senusret II, known from her tomb at Lahun, where a treasure of jewelry was found. She must have died under Amenemhat III, whose name appears on objects from her tomb.
