personas/sithathor/resumen.texto: Princess of the 12th Dynasty, daughter of the king, known only from her tomb at Dahshur, next to the pyramid of Senusret III. Two jewelry boxes escaped the notice of the robbers.

personas/neferuptah/resumen.texto: Daughter of Amenemhat III, of the 12th Dynasty, and sister of Queen Sobekneferu. Her pyramid, 2 km southeast of her father's at Hawara, was excavated in 1956.

personas/aat/resumen.texto: Queen of the 12th Dynasty, buried at Dahshur beneath her husband's pyramid, next to another queen, Khenemetneferhedjet III. Robbers plundered her tomb, but her sarcophagus, a false door and part of the grave goods remained.

personas/amenemhat-senebef/resumen.texto: King of the 13th Dynasty who, according to Ryholt, von Beckerath and Baker, was second in the list and reigned c. 1800–1796 BC. He may have governed from Itjtawy.

personas/nerikare/resumen.texto: King of the 13th Dynasty who, according to Ryholt and Baker, was third in the list and reigned briefly in 1796 BC; von Beckerath places him twenty-third.

personas/hotepibre-qemau/resumen.texto: King of the 13th Dynasty who, according to Ryholt and Baker, was sixth in the list and reigned from one to five years, possibly three, c. 1791–1788 BC.

personas/iufni/resumen.texto: King of the 13th Dynasty known only from the Turin Canon, compiled about five hundred years later. According to the reconstruction of the Canon he is placed around 1788 or around 1741 BC.

personas/nebnuni/resumen.texto: Poorly attested king of the 13th Dynasty, known mainly from his place in the Turin Canon. Ryholt gives him two years of reign, 1785–1783 BC, and assumes he was of non-royal origin; other Egyptologists give him one year, in 1739 BC.

personas/sehetepibre-sewesekhtawy/resume.texto: King of the 13th Dynasty who, according to Ryholt and Baker, was tenth in the list and reigned two years, from 1783 to 1781 BC; his exact position in the dynasty is disputed.

personas/sewadjkare-i/resumen.texto: King of the 13th Dynasty who, according to Ryholt and Baker, was eleventh in the list and reigned briefly around 1781 BC; other Egyptologists place him much later.

personas/nedjemibre/resumen.texto: Ephemeral king of the 13th Dynasty who reigned around 1780 or around 1736 BC. Ryholt and Baker make him twelfth in the list; Franke and von Beckerath make him eleventh.

personas/khaankhre-sobekhotep/resumen.texto: Minor king of the 13th Dynasty, whose chronological position is disputed: he was called Sobekhotep I and is now regarded as Sobekhotep II or Sobekhotep IV. Ryholt makes him Sobekhotep II and places him around 1780 BC.

personas/renseneb/resumen.texto: Poorly attested king of the 13th Dynasty; according to Ryholt he was fourteenth in the list, while Franke makes him thirteenth and von Beckerath sixteenth.

personas/hor-awibre/resumen.texto: King of the 13th Dynasty with a short reign, which the Turin Canon preserves in part and who may have been co-regent of Sekhemre Khutawy Khabaw. His tomb, found intact at Dahshur, contained his ka statue; he is placed c. 1777–1775 BC in one of the reconstructions.

personas/khabaw/resumen.texto: King of the 13th Dynasty well attested by archaeological finds, such as a red granite architrave from Bubastis. He may have been co-regent of Hor Awibre.

personas/djedkheperew/resumen.texto: King of the 13th Dynasty who, according to Ryholt and Baker, was seventeenth in the list and reigned two years, c. 1772–1770 BC. Djedkheperew is his Horus name.

personas/kay-amenemhat-vii/resumen.texto: King of the 13th Dynasty known from several objects, among them six cylinder seals and two scarabs, and from a graffito in the tomb of Queen Khuit I at Saqqara. It has been proposed to date him to around 1769–1766 BC.

personas/imyremeshaw/resumen.texto: Minor king of the 13th Dynasty with a short reign, attested mainly in the region of Memphis and the Fayum. He is said to have reigned from Memphis from 1759 or from 1711 BC.

personas/sehetepkare-intef/resumen.texto: Minor king of the 13th Dynasty who reigned from Memphis for less than ten years, between 1759 and 1749 BC or around 1710 BC, and is attested in the Fayum by a seated statue.

personas/seth-meribre/resumen.texto: King of the 13th Dynasty attested only in the Turin Canon, with no certain contemporary proof. He would have been twenty-fourth in the list and would have reigned from Memphis until 1749 or until c. 1700 BC.

personas/sihathor/resumen.texto: Ephemeral ruler of the 13th Dynasty, who perhaps never reigned on his own but only for a few months as co-regent of his brother Neferhotep I. According to Ryholt he died in 1733 BC; Franke dates his reign to 1694.

personas/merhotepre-sobekhotep/resumen.texto: King of the late 13th Dynasty, attested mainly in Upper Egypt; in older studies he was called Sobekhotep VI. His chronology is uncertain.

personas/sobekhotep-vi/resumen.texto: King of the late 13th Dynasty, perhaps a son of Sobekhotep IV, whom Ryholt places in 1719–1715 BC; he is also known as Sobekhotep V.

personas/merhotepre-ini/resumen.texto: Minor king of the 13th Dynasty who is regarded as the successor of Merneferre Ay. The Turin Canon gives him a reign of two years, three or four months and nine days.

personas/sankhenre-sewadjtu/resumen.texto: King of the 13th Dynasty, thirty-fourth in the list, who according to Ryholt reigned from Memphis from 1675 BC for three years and two to four months. He is known not from contemporary documents but only from royal lists.

personas/mersekhemre-ined/resumen.texto: King of the late 13th Dynasty, possibly thirty-fifth in the list, who would have reigned briefly from Memphis, from 1672 to 1669 BC or from 1651 to 1648 BC.

personas/merkawre-sobekhotep/resumen.texto: Minor king of the Second Intermediate Period with an uncertain chronological position. He probably reigned over Middle Egypt and perhaps Upper Egypt around 1664–1663 BC; Schneider dates him to 1646–1644.

personas/sewahenre-senebmiu/resumen.texto: Poorly attested king of the late 13th Dynasty, whose evidence all comes from Upper Egypt. Ryholt only specifies that his brief reign falls between 1660 and 1649 BC.

personas/yaammu/resumen.texto: Ruler of Asiatic descent in the Second Intermediate Period. Traditionally he is placed in the 16th Dynasty, as von Beckerath does, and Ryholt proposed that he was the second king of the 14th Dynasty, with about ten years of reign between 1780 and 1770 BC.

personas/qareh/resumen.texto: Possible third king of the 14th Dynasty, of Canaanite origin, who reigned from Avaris over the east of the Delta for about ten years, from 1770 to 1760 BC or later, around 1710. He may also have been a later vassal of the Hyksos kings of the 15th Dynasty.

personas/merdjefare/resumen.texto: King of the 14th Dynasty who is said to have reigned from Avaris over the east of the Delta, and perhaps over the west, around 1700 BC, for three or four years according to one reconstruction.

personas/nebsenre/resumen.texto: King of the 14th Dynasty who reigned at least five months over the east of the Delta, and perhaps the west, in the first half of the 17th century BC. His name appears in the Turin Canon, and he was contemporary with the 13th Dynasty, which governed from Memphis.

personas/sewadjkare-iii/resumen.texto: King of the 14th Dynasty, also called Sewadjkare II, who is said to have reigned from Avaris over the east of the Delta, and perhaps the west, around 1700 BC, for one year according to one reconstruction.

personas/semqen/resumen.texto: Hyksos ruler of Lower Egypt in the middle of the 17th century BC. Von Beckerath made him the third king of the 16th Dynasty and a vassal of the Hyksos of the 15th Dynasty, an opinion shared by Hayes and Helck and rejected by Ryholt.

personas/aperanat/resumen.texto: Ruler of Lower Egypt in the middle of the 17th century BC. Von Beckerath made him the second king of the 16th Dynasty and a vassal of the Hyksos of the 15th Dynasty, an opinion rejected by Ryholt.

personas/sakir-har/resumen.texto: Hyksos king from the beginning of the 15th Dynasty, who ruled part of Lower Egypt in the Second Intermediate Period.

personas/yanassi/resumen.texto: Hyksos prince, and possibly king, of the 15th Dynasty, eldest son of Khyan and perhaps his designated heir. He may be the “Iannas” of Manetho in Josephus's version.

personas/djehuty-sekhemre-sementawy/resu.texto: Minor king of Upper Egypt to whom the Turin Canon gives three years of reign. Ryholt and Baker place him in the 16th Dynasty, which controlled the Theban region after 1650 BC, and make him the predecessor of Sobekhotep VIII.

personas/sobekhotep-viii/resumen.texto: Ruler of the Second Intermediate Period with an uncertain chronological position, perhaps from the Theban region. It is disputed whether he belonged to the 13th, 16th or 17th Dynasty; Ryholt makes him reign from 1645 to 1629 BC. His only contemporary attestation is a flood stela found at the third pylon of Karnak.

personas/neferhotep-iii/resumen.texto: Third or fourth ruler of the Theban 16th Dynasty, after Sobekhotep VIII according to Ryholt and Baker. The Turin Canon gives him one year of reign, and he is known mainly from a stela from Thebes.

personas/mentuhotepi/resumen.texto: Pharaoh of the fragmented Second Intermediate Period, in Upper Egypt.

personas/nebiryraw-i/resumen.texto: King of the 16th Dynasty based at Thebes. The Legal Stela, dated to his year 1, is his main attestation.

personas/nebiryraw-ii/resumen.texto: Pharaoh of the 16th Dynasty based at Thebes, during the Second Intermediate Period.

personas/semenre/resumen.texto: Poorly attested Theban pharaoh who succeeded the equally obscure Nebiryraw II. According to Ryholt, who places him in the 16th Dynasty, he reigned from 1601 to 1600 BC; Franke places him in the 17th Dynasty, around 1580.

personas/bebiankh/resumen.texto: King of Upper Egypt during the Second Intermediate Period, often placed in the Theban 16th Dynasty. The Turin Canon gives him twelve years of reign.

personas/shedwaset/resumen.texto: Pharaoh of the Theban 16th Dynasty who is not attested in archaeology and appears only as a name in the Turin Canon.

personas/dedumose-i/resumen.texto: Pharaoh of the Second Intermediate Period who, according to Ryholt, Baker, Dodson and Hilton, reigned in the 16th Dynasty. Von Beckerath, Schneider and Franke place him in the 13th, with a reign ending around 1690 BC.

personas/dedumose-ii/resumen.texto: Pharaoh of the Second Intermediate Period who, according to Ryholt and Baker, reigned in the Theban 16th Dynasty. Von Beckerath, Schneider and Franke place him in the 13th Dynasty, with a reign ending around 1690 BC.

personas/merankhre-mentuhotep/resumen.texto: Theban king of the 16th Dynasty who may have been its fourteenth, known only from two statuettes.

personas/senusret-iv/resumen.texto: Theban king of the late Second Intermediate Period, attested only by finds from Upper Egypt; his chronological position and his dynasty are disputed.

personas/mentuhotep-reina/resumen.texto: Queen of the Second Intermediate Period, Great Royal Wife of the pharaoh Djehuty and daughter of the vizier Senebhenaf. Her coffin, now lost, was decorated on the inside with spells, many from the Book of the Dead.

personas/wepwawetemsaf/resumen.texto: Pharaoh of the Second Intermediate Period who, according to Ryholt and Baker, belonged to the Abydos dynasty, without a precise position within it.

personas/pantjeny/resumen.texto: Pharaoh of the Second Intermediate Period who, according to Ryholt and Baker, belonged to the Abydos dynasty, without a precise position within it.

personas/snaaib/resumen.texto: Pharaoh of the Second Intermediate Period, attested by a stela from Abydos (Kom es-Sultan) dedicated to the cult of Min-Horus-nakht.

personas/intef-v/resumen.texto: Pharaoh of the 17th Dynasty who lived at the end of the Second Intermediate Period, when Egypt was divided between Lower Egypt, controlled by the Hyksos, and Theban Upper Egypt; also called Intef V.

personas/intef-vii/resumen.texto: King of the 17th Dynasty, sometimes called Intef VII, who ruled during the Second Intermediate Period, when Egypt was divided between the Theban 17th Dynasty and the Hyksos 15th Dynasty.

personas/senajtenra-ahmose/resumen.texto: King of the 17th Dynasty who reigned briefly over the Theban region while the Hyksos of the 15th Dynasty dominated Lower Egypt, and died around 1560 or 1558 BC at the latest. He was remembered together with Seqenenre and Kamose among the Lords of the West, and he is identified with the husband of Tetisheri.

personas/sobekemsaf-reina/resumen.texto: Queen of the 17th Dynasty, wife of Nubkheperre Intef and sister of an unidentified pharaoh, probably Heruhirmaat Intef, Sobekemsaf II or Senakhtenre Ahmose. Her name is grammatically masculine, which is not unusual in the Second Intermediate Period.

personas/nubkhaes/resumen.texto: Queen of the Second Intermediate Period with the titles of Great Royal Wife and united with the beauty of the White Crown. Several of her relatives were officials of the late 13th Dynasty.

personas/haankhes/resumen.texto: Consort queen of the Second Intermediate Period of an unknown pharaoh, known only from the stela of her son, Prince Ameni, found at Koptos. Ameni married the princess Sobekemheb, daughter of Sobekemsaf I.

personas/ahmose-inhapy/resumen.texto: Princess and queen of the late 17th and early 18th Dynasties, probably daughter of Senakhtenre, sister of Seqenenre Tao and of the queens Ahhotep and Sitdjehuti, and wife of Seqenenre. She was the mother of Ahmose-Henuttamehu.

personas/sitdjehuti/resumen.texto: Princess and queen of the late 17th Dynasty, daughter of Senakhtenre Ahmose and Tetisheri, wife of her brother Seqenenre Tao and mother of Princess Ahmose. She died under Amenhotep I or Thutmose I.

personas/ahmose-henuttamehu/resumen.texto: Princess and queen of the late 17th and early 18th Dynasties, daughter of Seqenenre Tao and Ahmose Inhapy. She probably married her half-brother Ahmose I, and she was a half-sister of Ahmose-Nefertari.

personas/ahmose-nebetta/resumen.texto: Princess of the late 17th Dynasty, probably daughter of Seqenenre Tao and Ahhotep I and sister of the pharaoh Ahmose I.

personas/ahmose-princesa/resumen.texto: Daughter of Seqenenre Tao and Sitdjehuti and half-sister of Ahmose I and Ahmose-Nefertari. She was buried in QV47 in the Valley of the Queens, which is considered the first tomb built there.

personas/ahmose-tumerisy/resumen.texto: Princess of the late 17th Dynasty, probably daughter of Seqenenre Tao and sister of Ahmose I, judging by her titles of king's daughter and king's sister. She is known from her coffin, now in the Hermitage.

personas/sobeknakht-ii/resumen.texto: Nomarch of El Kab and supporter of the Theban 16th or 17th Dynasties, son and successor of Sobeknakht I. His tomb, one of the best preserved and most decorated of the Second Intermediate Period, records a great Nubian invasion, with allies from Punt and the Medjay, against the fragile Theban state.

personas/ahmose-si-tayit/resumen.texto: Possible first viceroy of Kush, under Ahmose I and Amenhotep I. Before him power in Kush seems to have been in the hands of Hormeni, mayor of Hierakonpolis; at the beginning of the reign of Amenhotep I he was succeeded by his son Turo.

personas/ahmose-turo/resumen.texto: Viceroy of Kush under Amenhotep I and Thutmose I, son of Si-Tayit, who had been commander of Buhen under Ahmose I. He appears in inscriptions from Semna and Uronarti and in others from years 1 and 3 of Thutmose I.

personas/inebny/resumen.texto: Viceroy of Kush under Queen Hatshepsut, attested in her years 18 and 20 and also called Amenemnekhu, at the head of the Nubian provinces.

personas/penre/resumen.texto: Viceroy of Kush under Hatshepsut, whose name is written Penre, Pare or Payre. He was little known until a Hungarian mission excavated his tomb at Thebes.

personas/amenhotep-virrey-de-kush/resume.texto: King's Son of Kush and chief administrator of the Nubian provinces, probably under Thutmose IV. A rock inscription from the island of Sehel records his titles.

personas/amenhotep-huy/resumen.texto: Viceroy of Kush under Tutankhamun, successor of Thutmose, who served with Akhenaten, and whom his son Paser I succeeded.

personas/amenemopet-virrey-de-kush/resum.texto: Viceroy of Kush under Seti I, son of the viceroy Paser I and grandson of Amenhotep called Huy. He was the king's first charioteer, and he is attested on the road from Aswan to Philae, at Buhen and at Sehel.

personas/setau/resumen.texto: Viceroy of Kush in the second half of the reign of Ramesses II, from year 38 at least until year 63. A long autobiography at Wadi es-Sebua recounts his career, and he built there the temple of Ramesses II and that of Gerf Hussein.

personas/huy-virrey-de-kush/resumen.texto: Viceroy of Kush under Ramesses II, before or after Setau, mayor of Tjaru and royal messenger to the Hittites. An inscription says that he escorted Queen Maathorneferure from Hatti to Egypt.

personas/messuy/resumen.texto: Viceroy of Kush and governor of the Southern Lands under Merneptah, and perhaps under Seti II and Amenmesse.

personas/wentawat/resumen.texto: Viceroy of Kush under Ramesses IX, son of the viceroy Nahihor. He is known from a stela in the British Museum (EA 792).

personas/pinehesy/resumen.texto: Viceroy of Kush under Ramesses XI. At an uncertain date in that reign he managed to remove the Theban high priest Amenhotep from office temporarily, the so-called war against the high priest. The papyri of the early years of the Renaissance era describe him as a public enemy.

personas/ahmose-reina/resumen.texto: Great Royal Wife of Thutmose I and mother of the queen and pharaoh Hatshepsut. Her name means “born of the Moon”.

personas/amenmose-principe/resumen.texto: Prince of the 18th Dynasty, eldest son and designated heir of Thutmose I.

personas/wadjmose/resumen.texto: Prince of the 18th Dynasty, son of the pharaoh Thutmose I.

personas/ahmose-ankh/resumen.texto: Crown prince during the reign of Ahmose I, at the beginning of the 18th Dynasty.

personas/siamun-hijo-de-ahmose-i/resumen.texto: Prince at the beginning of the 18th Dynasty, son of Ahmose I and Queen Ahmose-Nefertari. His mummy was found in the Deir el-Bahari cache (DB320) and is in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

personas/iset-reina/resumen.texto: Queen of the 18th Dynasty who received the name of the goddess Isis, a secondary wife or concubine of Thutmose II.

personas/satiah/resumen.texto: First Great Royal Wife of Thutmose III, whose name means “daughter of the Moon”.

personas/nebtu/resumen.texto: Wife of Thutmose III, shown on a pillar of his tomb KV34, where the king leads a procession of his family with his two Great Royal Wives, Meritra-Hatshepsut and Satiah, and his daughter Nefertari.

personas/menhet-menwi-y-merti/resumen.texto: Three lesser wives of Thutmose III, born abroad and perhaps Syrian to judge by their names. They are known from their rock-cut and richly equipped tomb in Wadi Gabbanat el-Qurud, near Luxor.

personas/amenemhat-hijo-de-tutmosis-iii/.texto: Prince of the 18th Dynasty, eldest son and designated heir of Thutmose III; his mother may have been Queen Satiah.

personas/tiaa/resumen.texto: Consort queen of the 18th Dynasty, a “faceless” concubine in the time of Amenhotep II, who denied her the title of Great Royal Wife. When her son Thutmose IV came to the throne, he reviewed her situation and granted it to her.

personas/iaret/resumen.texto: Great Royal Wife of the middle of the 18th Dynasty, daughter of Amenhotep II and wife of Thutmose IV. She was the second Great Royal Wife of that reign, and no children of hers are known.

personas/nefertari-dinastia-18/resumen.texto: First Great Royal Wife of Thutmose IV, of unknown and probably common origin. In several depictions she appears with the queen mother Tiaa as goddesses accompanying the king.

personas/webensenu/resumen.texto: Prince of the 18th Dynasty, son of Amenhotep II and brother of Thutmose IV. He died as a child, and he may have been buried in his father's tomb; a statue of Minmose mentions him.

personas/henuttaneb/resumen.texto: Princess of the 18th Dynasty, daughter of Amenhotep III and his Great Royal Wife Tiye.

personas/nebetah/resumen.texto: Daughter of Amenhotep III and his Great Royal Wife Tiye, younger sister of Akhenaten.

personas/iset-hija-de-amenhotep-iii/resu.texto: Princess of Egypt, daughter of Amenhotep III.

personas/neferneferuaten-tasherit/resume.texto: Princess of the 18th Dynasty, fourth daughter of Akhenaten and his Great Royal Wife Nefertiti.

personas/neferneferure/resumen.texto: Princess of the 18th Dynasty, the fifth of the six known daughters of Amenhotep IV and his Great Royal Wife Nefertiti.

personas/setepenre-princesa/resumen.texto: Egyptian princess of the 18th Dynasty, the last daughter of Akhenaten and Nefertiti.

personas/tey/resumen.texto: Great Royal Wife of Ay, the penultimate pharaoh of the 18th Dynasty, who had also been nurse of Nefertiti.

personas/amenia/resumen.texto: Egyptian noblewoman, first wife of Horemheb, the last ruler of the 18th Dynasty.

personas/dama-joven-kv35/resumen.texto: Informal name of a mummy found by Victor Loret in 1898 in tomb KV35 of the Valley of the Kings, designated KV35YL, which is preserved in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

personas/dakhamunzu/resumen.texto: Name of the widowed Egyptian queen who appears in the Deeds of Suppiluliuma, written by his son Mursili II. She has been identified with Nefertiti, Meritaten or Ankhesenamun, and it has been proposed that it is only the Hittite transcription of “the king's wife”.

personas/nehsi/resumen.texto: Official of Hatshepsut's court, probably of Nubian origin, who was bearer of the royal seal and chief treasurer. He appears in the Punt reliefs of the temple of Deir el-Bahari.

personas/djehuty-general/resumen.texto: General of Thutmose III in the 18th Dynasty, protagonist of the tale “The Capture of Joppa”. Drovetti found his tomb intact at Saqqara in 1824, and its objects were sold to collections around the world.

personas/useramen/resumen.texto: Vizier under Hatshepsut and Thutmose III, of the 18th Dynasty, also called User.

personas/puimre/resumen.texto: Nobleman, architect and second priest of Amun under Thutmose III. He was son of Puia and Nefer-iah and was married to Tanefert and to Sensonb, daughter of the high priest.

personas/menkheperreseneb-ii/resumen.texto: High priest of Amun, supervisor of the treasuries of gold and silver and chief of the supervisors of craftsmen under Thutmose III and Amenhotep II; he was perhaps buried in his Theban tomb TT112.

personas/sennefer/resumen.texto: Mayor of Thebes and supervisor of the granaries, fields, gardens and cattle of Amun under Amenhotep II, whose favourite he was and to whom he owed great wealth.

personas/maiherpri/resumen.texto: Noble of possible Nubian origin, buried in tomb KV36 of the Valley of the Kings, an honour reserved for few. He probably lived under Thutmose IV; his name means “lion of the battlefield”.

personas/kha/resumen.texto: Foreman and official of Deir el-Medina under Amenhotep II, Thutmose IV and Amenhotep III, with the titles of chief of the Great Place and supervisor of works; he directed the workers of the royal tombs and is often described as an architect. His burial chamber, together with that of his wife Merit, was found intact by Schiaparelli in 1906.

personas/paheri/resumen.texto: Provincial governor, royal tutor, treasury administrator and high-ranking priest of Upper Egypt, under Thutmose I, Thutmose II, Hatshepsut and Thutmose III.

personas/amenhotep-mayordomo-de-menfis/r.texto: Greatest steward of Memphis under Amenhotep III, one of the highest officials of the court.

personas/aperel/resumen.texto: Vizier with a Semitic name under Amenhotep III and Akhenaten, who was also commander of chariots.

personas/ptahmose-visir/resumen.texto: High priest of Amun and vizier of Upper Egypt under Amenhotep III; some historians place him at the end of the reign and others in its first part.

personas/khaemhat/resumen.texto: High official of Amenhotep III, also called Mahu, royal scribe and supervisor of the double granary of Upper and Lower Egypt, responsible for the palace food supplies.

personas/meryre-ii/resumen.texto: Amarna nobleman, steward of Queen Nefertiti, with the titles of royal scribe, steward, supervisor of the two treasuries and supervisor of the queen's harem. He had his tomb built at Amarna, and his mummy has not been identified.

personas/panehesy/resumen.texto: Amarna nobleman, first servant of the Aten in the Aten temple of Akhetaten and second prophet of the Lord of the Two Lands, who was also bearer of the seal of Lower Egypt and supervisor of the cattle and granary of the Aten.

personas/nakhtpaaten/resumen.texto: Vizier under Akhenaten, of the 18th Dynasty; his name means “the Aten is strong”.

personas/bek-escultor/resumen.texto: First chief royal sculptor under Akhenaten, son of Men, who held the same office under Amenhotep III, and of Roi, a woman from Heliopolis. He was raised in Heliopolis.

personas/usermontu/resumen.texto: Vizier from the reign of Tutankhamun until probably that of Horemheb. He appears in the tomb of Khonsu, called To (TT31), with his brother Huy, prophet of Montu, offering to the barque of Montu.

personas/mahu-oficial/resumen.texto: Official under Ramesses II, known mainly for his monumental tomb at Saqqara. He was royal scribe, greatest steward of Ptah, supervisor of the granary of the Lord of Truth and royal messenger to the land of Khatti, that is, to the Hittites.

personas/tuya-reina/resumen.texto: Wife of the pharaoh Seti I of the 19th Dynasty, whose name means “the admirable”. She is also named in the Hittite correspondence.

personas/maathorneferure/resumen.texto: Great Royal Wife of Ramesses II, a Hittite princess called by her Egyptian name, whom the king married thirteen years after the treaty. An inscription says that the viceroy Huy escorted her from Hatti.

personas/nebettawy/resumen.texto: Egyptian princess and queen, fifth daughter and one of the eight Great Royal Wives of Ramesses II.

personas/takhat/resumen.texto: Princess and queen of the 19th Dynasty, mother of the usurper Amenmesse. Little more is known of her; she held the titles of king's daughter and king's wife, and she may be the Takhat, daughter of Ramesses II, who appears in other sources.

personas/isetnofret-ii/resumen.texto: Woman of the Egyptian royal family, Great Royal Wife of Merneptah, for which reason she is called Isetnofret II.

personas/meryatum/resumen.texto: Prince and high priest of Ra, son of Ramesses II and Queen Nefertari; he appears sixteenth in the processions of princes and was probably the last child of the couple.

personas/bakenkhonsu/resumen.texto: High priest of Amun under Ramesses II. The inscription on the back of his cubic statue, now in Munich, reports on the education of young Egyptian nobles of his time.

personas/nebwenenef/resumen.texto: High priest of Amun at the beginning of the reign of Ramesses II, who had earlier been high priest of Anhur and of Hathor under Seti I and perhaps before.

personas/roma-roy/resumen.texto: High priest of Amun at the end of the reign of Ramesses II, under Merneptah and probably under Seti II. He had been third and then second priest of Amun before becoming first prophet.

personas/didia/resumen.texto: High priest of Ptah under Ramesses II, who succeeded his father Pahemnetjer in the office, probably in year 35 of the king, and held it for about fifteen years, until he was succeeded by Prince Khaemwaset.

personas/panehesy-visir/resumen.texto: Vizier of the 19th Dynasty under Merneptah.

personas/sennedjem/resumen.texto: Craftsman of Set Maat, today Deir el-Medina, under Seti I and Ramesses II, with the title of servant in the Place of Truth. He was buried with his wife in his tomb in the village.

personas/tiye-dinastia-20/resumen.texto: Secondary wife of Ramesses III who instigated the harem conspiracy against him. She is known from the Turin Judicial Papyrus, which records the trial.

personas/pebekkamen/resumen.texto: Official of Ramesses III who, with the secondary wife Tiye and the official Mesedsure, was one of the principal organizers of the harem conspiracy, whose aim was to murder the king.

personas/tyti/resumen.texto: Queen of the 20th Dynasty, wife and sister of Ramesses III, possibly mother of Ramesses IV.

personas/duatentopet/resumen.texto: Queen of the 20th Dynasty, wife of Ramesses IV and mother of Ramesses V; she is the most probable candidate on the basis of her titles, although the identity of the wife of Ramesses IV is not clearly stated.

personas/nubkhesbed/resumen.texto: Great Royal Wife of Ramesses VI and mother of Ramesses VII, of Princess Iset, God's Wife of Amun, and of the princes Amenherkhepeshef and Panebenkemyt. She is mentioned in the tomb of her son Amenherkhepeshef.

personas/amenherjepeshef-dinastia-20/res.texto: Eldest son and designated heir of Ramesses III, who bore the name of a son of Ramesses II. He died at about fifteen years of age, and his tomb is QV55.

personas/khaemwaset-dinastia-20/resumen.texto: Egyptian prince, son of Ramesses III, also called Ramesses Khaemwaset.

personas/khaemwaset-visir/resumen.texto: Vizier of the South and governor of Thebes, and perhaps high priest of Ptah, under Ramesses IX. He is known mainly because he ordered and directed the investigation of the robberies of royal tombs that took place at Thebes.

personas/piankh/resumen.texto: High priest of Amun, also royal scribe, son of the king of Kush and supervisor. He was once held to be the son and heir of Herihor, but recent studies show that he was his predecessor in the office.

personas/nodjmet/resumen.texto: Egyptian noblewoman of the late 20th and early 21st Dynasties, known mainly as the wife of Herihor, high priest of Amun at Thebes.

personas/tentamun-dinastia-20/resumen.texto: Queen of the 20th Dynasty, probably wife of Ramesses XI.

personas/esmendes/resumen.texto: Founder of the 21st Dynasty, who came to the throne after burying Ramesses XI in Lower Egypt, a territory he controlled. According to the Report of Wenamun, of around 1000 BC, he was governor of Lower Egypt during the Renaissance era.

personas/abdi-ashirta/resumen.texto: Ruler of Amurru, in conflict with King Rib-Hadda of Byblos in the Amarna Letters, and father of Aziru.

personas/biridiya/resumen.texto: King of Megiddo, a vassal city-state of Egypt in the 14th century BC, who was involved in Labaya's intrigues. He is one of the rulers who wrote the Amarna Letters.

personas/abimilki/resumen.texto: Prince of Tyre, called Surru in the letters, in the period of the Amarna Letters. He wrote ten letters to the pharaoh Amenhotep IV (EA 146–155), and in EA 147 the pharaoh confirmed him as ruler of the city.

personas/milkilu/resumen.texto: Ruler of Gezer around 1350 BC, son-in-law of Tagi and ally of Labaya in a period of unrest among Egypt's vassals. He was accused of rebellion and of employing Habiru mercenaries.

personas/akizzi/resumen.texto: King of Qatna around 1350–1345 BC, successor of Idanda and author of several Amarna Letters in which he asks the pharaoh for help against invaders.

personas/tushratta/resumen.texto: King of Mitanni from the end of the reign of Amenhotep III and during the first half of that of Amenhotep IV. He was son of Shuttarna II and grandson of Artatama I; his sister Gilukhepa and his daughter Tadukhepa married pharaohs.

personas/suppiluliuma-i/resumen.texto: Hittite king, who reigned c. 1350–1322 BC. Before coming to the throne he had distinguished himself as a military commander, protecting and recovering Hittite territories after foreign attacks, and afterwards he pursued his programme of conquests.

personas/hattusili-iii/resumen.texto: King (labarna) of the Hittite Empire c. 1275–1245 BC according to the middle chronology, or 1267–1237 according to the short one. He was brother of Muwatalli II, who had appointed him governor of Hattusa, and he deposed his nephew Mursili III.

personas/puduhepa/resumen.texto: Hittite queen of Hattusili III, who has been called one of the most influential women known from the ancient Near East.

personas/muwatalli-ii/resumen.texto: King of the Hittite Empire c. 1295–1272 BC according to the middle chronology, known for moving the capital to Tarhuntassa, appointing his brother Hattusili governor of Hattusa and fighting Ramesses II at the battle of Qadesh.

personas/mursili-iii/resumen.texto: Hittite king, also called Urhi-Teshub, who reigned c. 1282–1275 BC according to the middle chronology and whom his uncle Hattusili III deposed and exiled to Syria. After his conspiracies to recover the throne failed, he fled to Egypt, the enemy country of the Hittites.

hechos/fundacion-de-itjtauy/resumen.texto: Amenemhat I founds a new capital, Itjtawy, near el-Lisht, south of Memphis, as the seat of the 12th Dynasty. The city has not been excavated and is known from texts and the nearby necropolis.

hechos/dinastia-12-de-egipto/resumen.texto: Dynasty of seven kings and one queen, from Amenemhat I to Sobekneferu, ruling from Itjtawy c. 1985–1773 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). Most Egyptologists accept coregencies among several kings, although their duration is disputed.

hechos/expedicion-de-henenu-a-punt/resum.texto: An inscription from Wadi Hammamat records an expedition of about three thousand men under the steward Henenu toward the Red Sea and Punt, in the reign of Mentuhotep III. It is the first documented Middle Kingdom mission to Punt.

hechos/expediciones-a-punt-desde-mersa-g.texto: Expeditions to Punt from Mersa Gawasis

Stelae and remains of ships found at Mersa Gawasis document that the kings of the 12th Dynasty sent expeditions by the Red Sea to Punt. The ships were taken apart to be carried overland and were assembled again on the coast.

hechos/fortalezas-de-la-segunda-catarata.texto: Egyptian Fortresses of the Second Cataract

The kings of the 12th Dynasty built a chain of mudbrick fortresses at the Second Cataract, such as Buhen, Mirgissa, Uronarti, Askut and Semna. They aimed to control the passage of the Nile and the trade to the south.

hechos/campanas-nubias-y-estelas-de-semn.texto: Senusret III's Nubian Campaigns and the Semna Stelae
Senusret III campaigns in Nubia, moves the frontier to Semna and has stelae erected that forbid Nubians to pass north with livestock. The campaigns are dated to his years 8, 10, 16 and 19.

hechos/campana-de-sesostris-iii-en-sique.texto: The stela of the official Sebek-khu, found at Abydos, recounts a campaign in the land of Sekmem, which is associated with Shechem; Peet published it in 1914 as the earliest record of an Egyptian campaign in Asia, although the earlier Annals of Amenemhat II already record the destruction of Iuai and Iasy. Its date within the reign and its scale are disputed.

hechos/llegada-de-asiaticos-en-beni-hasa.texto: Scene of Asiatics in the Tomb of Khnumhotep II

A painting in the tomb of the nomarch Khnumhotep II at Beni Hasan shows a group of Asiatics with their goods arriving in Egypt, dated to year 6 of Senusret II. It is a source for the Semitic presence in Egypt before the Hyksos.

hechos/obras-hidraulicas-del-fayum/titul.texto: Amenemhat III's Water Works in the Faiyum

hechos/obras-hidraulicas-del-fayum/resum.texto: Amenemhat III promotes the regulation of the water of the Faiyum with dikes and canals to gain arable land. He founded temples in the region and had himself buried there.

hechos/piramide-de-sesostris-ii-en-lahun.texto: Pyramid of Senusret II at Lahun
Senusret II builds his pyramid at Lahun, at the entrance to the Faiyum, with a core of natural rock and mudbrick. Beside it rose the workers' town of Kahun.

hechos/piramide-de-amenemhat-iii-en-hawa.texto: Pyramid of Amenemhat III at Hawara
Amenemhat III has a second pyramid built, at Hawara, after the problems with his first one at Dahshur. Beside it stood the great funerary temple that the Greeks called the Labyrinth.

hechos/piramide-negra-de-dahshur/titulo.texto: Black Pyramid of Amenemhat III at Dahshur

hechos/piramide-negra-de-dahshur/resumen.texto: Amenemhat III builds his first pyramid at Dahshur with mudbrick and a stone casing. It was abandoned because of subsidence and seepage, and another was built at Hawara.

hechos/escritura-protosinaitica/resumen.texto: Inscriptions in an alphabet of few signs derived from Egyptian hieroglyphs were found in the turquoise mines of Serabit el-Khadim. They are usually considered the origin of the Semitic alphabets, and their dating, between the 19th and 15th centuries BC, is disputed.

hechos/dinastia-13-de-egipto/resumen.texto: Long series of kings with short reigns, to which the Turin Canon gives fifty-three names, which follows the 12th Dynasty without a known heir of Sobekneferu. Shaw makes it begin c. 1773 BC and Ryholt c. 1803 and end in 1649; Neferhotep I and Sobekhotep IV are among the best attested, and around 1650 BC power passes to the south, to Thebes.

hechos/dinastia-14-de-egipto/resumen.texto: Dynasty that, according to Ryholt, governed the east of the Delta from Avaris c. 1805–1650 BC (Shaw makes it begin in 1773) and had kings of Levantine origin. The date and identity of several of its kings are disputed.

hechos/dinastia-16-de-egipto/resumen.texto: According to Ryholt, a Theban dynasty contemporary with the Hyksos that dominated Upper Egypt. Others identify it with the lesser Hyksos, and the list of the Turin Canon is damaged.

hechos/dinastia-de-abidos/resumen.texto: Independent kingdom in Upper Egypt, contemporary with the 15th and 16th Dynasties, whose existence Ryholt proposed and which the tomb of Senebkay, found in 2014, supports; Ilin-Tomich objects that Senebkay might belong to the 16th Dynasty.

hechos/dinastia-17-de-egipto/resumen.texto: Theban dynasty that governed Upper Egypt against the Hyksos of Avaris and the Nubians of Kerma, with Seqenenre Tao and Kamose at the end. It ends with Kamose and the accession of Ahmose I, c. 1550 BC; the capture of Avaris came years later, already in the 18th Dynasty.

hechos/apogeo-de-kerma/titulo.texto: Kingdom of Kush with Its Capital at Kerma

hechos/apogeo-de-kerma/resumen.texto: Kerma, at the Third Cataract, is the capital of a Nubian kingdom that dominated Upper Nubia and came to control the Nile as far as the Second Cataract. The texts of Kamose show Apepi seeking its alliance against Thebes, with an intercepted letter.

hechos/guerra-de-kamose-contra-los-hicso.texto: Kamose sails down the Nile northward with his fleet against the Hyksos king Apepi at Avaris, and the stelae of Karnak tell of his advance as far as Neferusi and the interception of a messenger of Apepi to the ruler of Kush. Ahmose I ended the war after his death.

hechos/redaccion-del-papiro-rhind/resume.texto: The scribe Ahmes copies, in year 33 of the Hyksos king Apepi, a mathematical text written in the time of Amenemhat III. The dating of the copy depends on the identification of Awserre with Apepi.

hechos/toma-de-sharuhen/resumen.texto: After the fall of Avaris, Ahmose I besieges Sharuhen, in southern Canaan, for three years, according to the autobiography of Ahmose son of Ebana. Its location is uncertain, and several sites have been proposed (Tell el-Ajjul, Tell el-Far'ah South, Tel Haror); Tell el-Ajjul is an approximation.

hechos/comienzo-de-la-dinastia-18/titulo.texto: Beginning of the 18th Dynasty and the New Kingdom

hechos/comienzo-de-la-dinastia-18/resume.texto: With the accession of Ahmose I, Thebes rules all of Egypt and the New Kingdom and the 18th Dynasty begin, c. 1550–1295 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). Its kings extend the domination to Nubia and the Levant.

hechos/campanas-de-ahmose-i-en-nubia/res.texto: After the war against the Hyksos, Ahmose I leads the army to Nubia, according to the autobiography of Ahmose son of Ebana. He restores the Egyptian frontier at the Second Cataract.

hechos/campana-de-tutmosis-i-contra-kush.texto: Thutmose I's Campaign in Nubia and the Tombos Stela

In year 2 of Thutmose I, a stela from Tombos records the construction of a fortress near the Third Cataract, after the victory over Kush. It is associated with the end of the independent kingdom of Kerma and with the viceroyalty of Kush, whose holder Turi was already in office under Amenhotep I and continued under Thutmose I.

hechos/campana-de-tutmosis-i-en-siria/ti.texto: Thutmose I's Campaign to the Euphrates

hechos/campana-de-tutmosis-i-en-siria/re.texto: Thutmose I leads the army to the Euphrates, according to the autobiographies of his officials, and has a stela erected on the river. Egypt does not maintain control of that region.

hechos/virreinato-de-kush/titulo.texto: Creation of the Viceroyalty of Kush

hechos/virreinato-de-kush/resumen.texto: Egypt organizes Nubia as a province governed by a viceroy, the “King's Son of Kush”, with centres at Aniba (Wawat) and Soleb, and later Amara West (Kush). The first may have been Ahmose called Si-Tayit, under Ahmose I, who was followed by his son Turi, already in office under Amenhotep I.

hechos/valle-de-los-reyes-primera-tumba/.texto: Beginning of Royal Burials in the Valley of the Kings

From Thutmose I, or perhaps already from Amenhotep I, the kings of the New Kingdom had themselves buried in rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the Kings and not in pyramids. At least sixty-three tombs are counted, and sixty-five with the chambers found from 2005 to 2008, of which some twenty are royal.

hechos/expedicion-de-hatshepsut-a-punt/r.texto: The reliefs of Hatshepsut's temple at Deir el-Bahari show the expedition of five ships to Punt by the Red Sea, led by the chancellor Nehsi, from which they bring back incense, myrrh and trees. The port of departure was probably Mersa Gawasis, where cedar planks from the expedition were found. It is dated to year 9 of her reign.

hechos/campana-de-tutmosis-iii-contra-qa.texto: Thutmose III's Campaigns against Kadesh and Syria
Thutmose III's fifth to seventh campaigns, around his years 29–31, target the Phoenician cities and Kadesh, on the Orontes. The date depends on the chronology, which the Annals fix in regnal years.

hechos/campana-de-tutmosis-iii-contra-mi.texto: In his eighth campaign, around year 33, Thutmose III crosses the Euphrates against Mitanni and, according to the Annals, has a stela erected. He is the first pharaoh since Thutmose I to do so.

hechos/campanas-de-amenhotep-ii-en-siria.texto: Amenhotep II campaigns in Syria in his years 3, 7 and 9: in year 3 he kills seven rebel princes and crosses the Orontes, and in year 9 he reaches Galilee and declares 101,128 captives, a figure that is disputed. After these campaigns hostilities between Egypt and Mitanni cease.

hechos/matrimonio-de-tutmosis-iv-con-una.texto: Thutmose IV's Marriage to a Princess of Mitanni

Thutmose IV establishes peaceful relations with Mitanni and marries a daughter of Artatama, after several requests, according to a letter from Tushratta to Akhenaten. It marks the end of the war over Syria.

hechos/matrimonio-de-amenhotep-iii-con-g.texto: Amenhotep III's Marriage to Gilukhepa of Mitanni
In year 10 of Amenhotep III, Gilukhepa, daughter of Shuttarna II of Mitanni, arrives in Egypt to marry the king. It was one of the diplomatic marriages of Amenhotep III.

hechos/templo-de-luxor/titulo.texto: Construction of the Temple of Luxor

hechos/templo-de-luxor/resumen.texto: Amenhotep III builds the temple of Luxor, dedicated to Amun, over a chapel of Hatshepsut. Ramesses II enlarged it with a court and obelisks.

hechos/templo-de-soleb/resumen.texto: Amenhotep III erects at Soleb a temple of Amun and of himself in Nubia. Its reliefs include lists of defeated peoples.

hechos/colosos-de-memnon-y-templo-funera.texto: Funerary Temple of Amenhotep III and the Colossi of Memnon

The funerary temple of Amenhotep III, on the west bank of Thebes, was one of the largest in Egypt, and today the two colossi at its entrance still stand. Part of it was later dismantled for other works.

hechos/restauracion-de-tutankamon/titulo.texto: Restoration of the Cults under Tutankhamun

hechos/restauracion-de-tutankamon/resume.texto: A stela of Tutankhamun at Karnak says that the king restored the temples and resumed the worship of the gods, which had been neglected; it does not name Akhenaten. Under Tutankhamun the court returns to Memphis and Thebes and the city of Amarna is abandoned, and the following kings erase Akhenaten from the royal lists.

hechos/asunto-de-zannanza/titulo.texto: Request by an Egyptian Queen for a Hittite Prince

hechos/asunto-de-zannanza/resumen.texto: According to the Deeds of Suppiluliuma, written by his son Mursili II, a widowed queen of Egypt, the “Dahamunzu”, asks Suppiluliuma I, who was besieging Carchemish, for one of his sons as a husband. Prince Zannanza died on the way; the queen is identified with Ankhesenamun, Nefertiti or Meritaten without agreement, and it has been proposed that Dahamunzu is only the Hittite transcription of “the king's wife”.

hechos/edicto-de-horemheb/resumen.texto: Horemheb issues a decree that punishes abuses by officials and soldiers against the people and reorganizes justice. It was found beside the tenth pylon of Karnak, where it is inscribed on a stela.

hechos/comienzo-de-la-dinastia-19/resume.texto: Ramesses I, a soldier of non-royal origin appointed by Horemheb, begins the 19th Dynasty, c. 1295–1186 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). His family came from the eastern Delta.

hechos/campanas-de-seti-i/titulo.texto: Seti I's Campaigns in Syria and Palestine

hechos/campanas-de-seti-i/resumen.texto: Seti I recovers territories of Canaan and takes Kadesh and Amurru from the Hittites, although he does not keep them. A stela from Beth Shean documents his campaign in Canaan.

hechos/sala-hipostila-de-karnak/resumen.texto: Seti I and Ramesses II build the hypostyle hall of the temple of Amun at Karnak, with 134 columns. It is one of the largest halls of any Egyptian temple.

hechos/templo-funerario-de-ramses-ii/res.texto: Ramesses II has the Ramesseum built in West Thebes as his funerary temple. Its walls show scenes of Kadesh and the remains of a colossal statue.

hechos/matrimonio-de-ramses-ii-con-una-p.texto: Ramesses II's Marriage to a Hittite Princess
Thirteen years after the treaty, Ramesses II marries a daughter of Hattusili III, according to stelae from Abu Simbel and Karnak. She was the princess known by her Egyptian name, Maathorneferure.

hechos/guerra-de-merenptah-contra-los-li.texto: In year 5 of Merneptah, Libyans, with help from the Sea Peoples, threaten the western Delta, and the Egyptian army defeats them in a six-hour battle at Perire. Merneptah records it in the Great Karnak Inscription, a mural text, and on his stela.

hechos/campana-de-merenptah-en-canaan/ti.texto: Merneptah's Campaign in Canaan and the Israel Stela

hechos/campana-de-merenptah-en-canaan/re.texto: The stela of Merneptah mentions the conquest of Ashkelon, Gezer, Yanoam and “Israel”, which according to the text is destroyed. It is the earliest mention of Israel generally accepted; an earlier reading on a Berlin pedestal is disputed.

hechos/disputa-sucesoria-de-amenmeses/ti.texto: Reign of Amenmesse and Dispute with Seti II

hechos/disputa-sucesoria-de-amenmeses/re.texto: Amenmesse occupies the throne at Thebes and in Nubia for some years, while Seti II remains in the north, according to one theory. The interpretation of the rivalry is disputed because the documents are scarce.

hechos/tutela-de-tausert-y-bay-sobre-sip.texto: Tausert and Chancellor Bay Govern in the Name of Siptah
Siptah comes to the throne as a child and rules under the guardianship of Tausert and the chancellor Bay, whom the king orders executed in his year 5. Tausert reigns in her own right after his death.

hechos/restauracion-del-orden-por-setnaj.texto: Setnakht ends a period of disorder and of the presence of foreigners, according to his Elephantine Stela and Papyrus Harris I, and founds the 20th Dynasty, c. 1186–1069 BC. The place is approximate (his stela is at Elephantine). It is disputed how he came to the throne and whether he was of the Ramesside line.

hechos/guerras-libias-de-ramses-iii/titu.texto: Ramesses III's Wars against the Libyans

hechos/guerras-libias-de-ramses-iii/resu.texto: Ramesses III repels the Libyans in the western Delta in his years 5 and 11, as the reliefs of Medinet Habu record. The Libyan groups later became mercenaries.

hechos/expediciones-de-ramses-iii-a-punt.texto: Ramesses III's Expeditions to Punt and Sinai
Papyrus Harris I says that Ramesses III sent expeditions to Punt, to the copper mines of Atika and to the turquoise mines of Sinai. The identification of Atika with Timna is disputed.

hechos/huelga-de-deir-el-medina/titulo.texto: Strike of the Workers of Deir el-Medina

hechos/huelga-de-deir-el-medina/resumen.texto: In year 29 of Ramesses III, the workers of the tombs stopped working because they were not receiving their rations and protested at West Thebes. The scribe of the necropolis recorded the events on a papyrus.

hechos/conspiracion-del-harem/resumen.texto: A conspiracy led by Tiye, a secondary wife, and palace officials, who wanted to put her son, Prince Pentaur, on the throne, ends in a trial whose names and sentences are preserved in the Turin Judicial Papyrus. It is disputed whether the king died in the attack.

hechos/fin-del-dominio-egipcio-en-canaan.texto: End of Egyptian Rule in Canaan

Around 1130 BC, under Ramesses VI or shortly after, the Egyptian military presence in Canaan is lost, including in garrisons such as that of Beth Shean. Egyptologists link the end to the crisis at the close of the Late Bronze Age and to internal weakness.

hechos/ascenso-de-herihor/titulo.texto: Herihor, High Priest of Amun, Takes Royal Titulary

hechos/ascenso-de-herihor/resumen.texto: Under Ramesses XI, Herihor concentrates the offices of high priest and military command and appears with royal titulary at Karnak. The division between Thebes and the Delta that follows is the basis of the Third Intermediate Period.

hechos/viaje-de-unamon-a-biblos/resumen.texto: In year 5 of the “Renaissance era”, under Ramesses XI according to the date usually given to it (the discussion dates from when Jansen-Winkeln reversed the order of Herihor and Piankh), Wenamun travels from Karnak to Byblos to buy cedar wood and is badly received. It is disputed whether the text is a real report or literature.

hechos/fin-del-dominio-egipcio-en-nubia/.texto: End of the Egyptian Viceroyalty of Kush

Towards the end of the reign of Ramesses XI, Egyptian rule over Nubia is lost: the viceroy Pinehesy temporarily removes the high priest of Amun Amenhotep from office, in what is called the war against the high priest, and Piankh undertakes a campaign against him. The papyri of the early years of the Renaissance era describe him as a public enemy, a distant figure.

hechos/fundacion-de-napata/resumen.texto: Thutmose III founds at Napata a fortified settlement (menenu) as the southern limit of the empire, and the temples of Amun at Jebel Barkal were built there throughout the New Kingdom. Napata later became the centre of the Nubian kingdom of Kush.

hechos/fundacion-de-sesebi/resumen.texto: Akhenaten founds in Nubia the city of Sesebi, with a temple of the Aten, which served as an administrative centre. Its buildings were abandoned shortly afterwards.

hechos/templo-funerario-de-mentuhotep-ii.texto: Funerary Temple of Mentuhotep II at Deir el-Bahari
Mentuhotep II has a terraced funerary temple built at Deir el-Bahari, with his tomb cut into the rock behind it. Hatshepsut later took it as the model for her own temple, next to it.

hechos/capilla-blanca-de-sesostris-i/tit.texto: White Chapel of Senusret I at Karnak

hechos/capilla-blanca-de-sesostris-i/res.texto: Senusret I has a limestone kiosk erected at Karnak for his jubilee, in his year 30. It was later dismantled and reused as filling in the third pylon, from where it was recovered and rebuilt. It is among the best-preserved architectural works of the Middle Kingdom.

hechos/piramides-de-amenemhat-i-y-sesost.texto: Pyramids of Amenemhat I and Senusret I at el-Lisht
Amenemhat I and Senusret I have their pyramids built at el-Lisht, next to the capital Itjtawy. They reuse blocks from monuments of the Old Kingdom.

hechos/templo-de-seti-i-en-abidos/titulo.texto: Temple of Seti I at Abydos

hechos/templo-de-seti-i-en-abidos/resume.texto: Seti I has built at Abydos a temple dedicated to Osiris and other gods, in whose corridor is the Abydos King List. Ramesses II completed it and built another temple beside it.

hechos/muros-del-gobernante/resumen.texto: Amenemhat I has a fortification, or a chain of them, built in the 14th nome of Lower Egypt to protect Egypt's eastern approaches; it succeeded the Walls of Snefru. The Story of Sinuhe and the Prophecy of Neferti mention them, and no remains have been found.

hechos/inscripciones-alfabeticas-de-wadi.texto: Two rock inscriptions from a valley between Thebes and Hiw which, according to John and Deborah Darnell, who found them in 1993, are the oldest known alphabet, from c. 1900–1800 BC. They are linked to the Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions.

hechos/piramide-de-amenemhat-i/titulo.texto: Pyramid of Amenemhat I at el-Lisht

hechos/piramide-de-amenemhat-i/resumen.texto: Amenemhat I has his pyramid built at el-Lisht, which returns to the size and form of Old Kingdom pyramids and introduces the custom of giving each building of the complex its own name.

hechos/piramide-blanca-de-amenemhat-ii/t.texto: White Pyramid of Amenemhat II at Dahshur

hechos/piramide-blanca-de-amenemhat-ii/r.texto: Amenemhat II has the White Pyramid built at Dahshur, today a heap of rubble because it was used as a quarry, inside a large rectangular enclosure where intact tombs were found.

hechos/piramide-de-sesostris-iii-en-dahs.texto: Pyramid of Senusret III at Dahshur
Senusret III has himself built at Dahshur, 1.5 km northeast of the Red Pyramid of Snefru, the northernmost of the pyramids of the site, with a mudbrick core faced with white limestone from Tura.

hechos/barcas-de-dahshur/resumen.texto: Group of five or six funerary boats found near the funerary complex of Senusret III, of the 12th Dynasty.

hechos/laberinto-de-hawara/resumen.texto: Structure or temple south of the pyramid of Amenemhat III at Hawara, perhaps a multipurpose building with palace, town and administrative centre. Visitors in the classical period compared it with the Labyrinth of Minos at Knossos.

hechos/piramide-meridional-de-mazghuna/r.texto: Unfinished royal tomb of the 12th or 13th Dynasty at Mazghuna, 5 km south of Dahshur, whose owner is unknown because no inscriptions were found. It was rediscovered by Mackay in 1910 and excavated by Petrie the following year.

hechos/piramide-de-ameny-qemau/titulo.texto: Pyramid of Ameny Qemau at Dahshur South

hechos/piramide-de-ameny-qemau/resumen.texto: Ameny Qemau, a little-known king of the 13th Dynasty, has his pyramid built in the south of Dahshur.

hechos/piramide-de-khendjer/titulo.texto: Pyramid of Khendjer at Saqqara South

hechos/piramide-de-khendjer/resumen.texto: Khendjer, of the 13th Dynasty, has a pyramid of about 37 m in height built, now in ruins, within a complex with a funerary temple, chapel, two enclosures and a subsidiary pyramid.

hechos/piramide-inconclusa-de-saqqara-su.texto: Unfinished royal tomb of the 13th Dynasty, notable for having the most elaborate underground complex since the pyramids of the late 12th Dynasty. Its owner is not known with certainty.

hechos/cultura-pan-grave/resumen.texto: Archaeological culture of the Middle Bronze Age of Egypt, Nubia and perhaps the eastern desert, which appears at the end of the Middle Kingdom and is more prominent in the Second Intermediate Period. Some of its members may have served as mercenaries in the wars of that period; it was formerly identified with the Medjay.

hechos/los-medjay/resumen.texto: Ethnonym that first designated a nomadic group of Nubia, already mentioned in the autobiography of Weni, and later the desert police. Senusret III forbade the passage of Nubians north of Semna, as recorded in the dispatches of the border guard at Elephantine; the Medjay were sometimes confused with the Pan-Grave culture.

hechos/tumba-de-tutmosis-ii-descubierta/.texto: Tomb of Thutmose II in Wadi C-4
Royal tomb C-4 in Wadi Gabbanat el-Qurud, west of Luxor, belonged to Thutmose II and has no mummy, which may have been in the royal cache of 1881. It was found in 2025.

hechos/capilla-roja-de-hatshepsut/titulo.texto: Red Chapel of Hatshepsut at Karnak

hechos/capilla-roja-de-hatshepsut/resume.texto: Hatshepsut had a shrine for the sacred barque built at Karnak. It was dismantled in antiquity and its parts were reused in other buildings; it was reconstructed from them.

hechos/obelisco-inconcluso-de-asuan/resu.texto: Granite obelisk of 41,75 m and about 1168 tonnes, the largest known, which was left in place in the Aswan quarries. Engelbach, who studied it in 1922, and other Egyptologists attribute it to Hatshepsut.

hechos/obelisco-de-letran/resumen.texto: Thutmose III had two obelisks carved, one for himself and one for his father, which were not finished when he died; Thutmose IV erected the one at Karnak, which is the largest ancient obelisk still standing. In 357 Constantius II took it to Rome.

hechos/obelisco-de-teodosio/resumen.texto: Obelisk of Thutmose III, erected around 1450 BC, which the emperor Theodosius had raised again in the Hippodrome of Constantinople.

hechos/agujas-de-cleopatra/resumen.texto: Pair of obelisks made at Heliopolis in the New Kingdom, inscribed by Thutmose III and by Ramesses II. In 13-12 BC they were taken to the Caesareum of Alexandria; today they are in London and New York.

hechos/asedio-de-dapur/titulo.texto: Siege of Dapur by Ramesses II

hechos/asedio-de-dapur/resumen.texto: Ramesses II besieges Dapur during his campaign to subdue Galilee and conquer Syria, which he recorded on a wall of the Ramesseum. The inscriptions say Dapur was in the land of Hatti, and Kitchen argues that it was not Tabor of Canaan but a city in Syria north of Kadesh; the location is approximate.

hechos/wehem-mesut/resumen.texto: Period of Egyptian history called wehem mesut, “repetition of births”, or the Renaissance Era, which begins in year 19 of Ramesses XI. The Mayer Papyri record the court sessions of its first two years.

hechos/colapso-de-la-edad-del-bronce-fin.texto: Period of social collapse in the eastern Mediterranean between the late 13th and early 12th centuries BC, which affected above all Egypt, Anatolia, the Aegean, eastern Libya and the Balkans. The palace economies of the Aegean and Anatolia fragmented and the Hittite Empire fell, while Assyria and Egypt survived weakened; the causes are the subject of rival theories.

lugares/itjtauy/resumen.texto: Capital founded by Amenemhat I c. 1985 BC in the El Lisht area, south of Memphis, and seat of the 12th Dynasty and much of the 13th. Its exact location has not been excavated; it is placed near the El Lisht necropolis.

lugares/el-lisht/resumen.texto: Necropolis of the 12th Dynasty next to Itjtauy, with the pyramids of Amenemhat I and Sesostris I and the tombs of their officials.

lugares/lahun/resumen.texto: Site at the entrance to the Fayum with the pyramid of Sesostris II and the workers' town called Kahun, from which the Kahun Papyri come. The town was occupied during the 12th Dynasty and the beginning of the 13th.

lugares/hawara/resumen.texto: Fayum necropolis with the pyramid of Amenemhat III and the funerary complex that classical authors called the Labyrinth.

lugares/buhen/resumen.texto: Site in the Second Cataract where there was an Egyptian settlement with copper workshops from the Old Kingdom, and where the 12th Dynasty, under Sesostris III, built a fortress that was the base of Egyptian rule over Nubia. Today it lies beneath Lake Nasser, after part of its temple was moved.

lugares/semna/resumen.texto: Fortress of the 12th Dynasty on the southern frontier set by Sesostris III, with border stelae and a record of Nile floods. It lies beneath Lake Nasser.

lugares/mirgissa/resumen.texto: Egyptian fortress of the 12th Dynasty at the Second Cataract, which controlled river traffic. It was excavated before the flooding of Lake Nasser, and deposits of execration rituals were found.

lugares/uronarti/resumen.texto: Island fortress of the 12th Dynasty at the Second Cataract, from the time of Sesostris III. It was part of the chain of fortresses on the southern frontier.

lugares/askut/resumen.texto: Island fortress of the 12th Dynasty south of the Second Cataract, with granaries. It was excavated before the creation of Lake Nasser.

lugares/kerma/resumen.texto: Capital of the kingdom of Kush at the Third Cataract, center of the Kerma culture, with large tombs and the great mudbrick structure called the “deffufa”. It was occupied by Egypt in the time of Thutmose I.

lugares/mersa-gawasis/resumen.texto: Egyptian Red Sea port used in the Middle Kingdom for expeditions to Punt. Anchors, ropes, ship timbers and official stelae were found there.

lugares/serabit-el-khadim/resumen.texto: Turquoise mining site in Sinai with a temple of Hathor founded under Sesostris I, c. 1950 BC, and enlarged in the New Kingdom. The Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions were found there.

lugares/beni-hasan/resumen.texto: Necropolis of Middle Kingdom nomarchs in Middle Egypt, with tombs decorated like those of Khnumhotep II and Amenemhat.

lugares/deir-el-bersha/resumen.texto: Necropolis of the nomarchs of the Hare nome in Middle Egypt, with the tombs of Djehutihotep and other Middle Kingdom nomarchs.

lugares/karnak/resumen.texto: Great temple complex at Thebes, center of the cult of Amun from the Middle Kingdom and enlarged by nearly all the kings of the New Kingdom.

lugares/templo-de-luxor/resumen.texto: Temple of Amun at Thebes built mainly by Amenhotep III and enlarged by Ramesses II. It was linked to Karnak by an avenue of sphinxes.

lugares/medinet-habu/resumen.texto: Temple complex on the West Bank at Thebes, with an earlier 18th-Dynasty temple and the mortuary temple that Ramesses III built c. 1180 BC on the model of the Ramesseum, with reliefs of his wars against the Libyans and the Sea Peoples.

lugares/ramesseo/resumen.texto: Mortuary temple of Ramesses II on the West Bank at Thebes, with the remains of a colossal statue of the king and reliefs of the Battle of Kadesh.

lugares/valle-de-los-reyes/resumen.texto: Royal necropolis of the New Kingdom on the West Bank at Thebes, with more than sixty tombs cut into the rock, from Thutmose I to Ramesses XI.

lugares/valle-de-las-reinas/resumen.texto: Necropolis of queens and princes of the 18th to 20th Dynasties on the West Bank at Thebes, with the tomb of Nefertari.

lugares/deir-el-bahari/resumen.texto: Rocky amphitheater on the West Bank at Thebes, with the mortuary temples of Mentuhotep II and Hatshepsut and the cache of royal mummies.

lugares/avaris/resumen.texto: City in the eastern Delta that was the capital of the Hyksos of the 15th Dynasty, with a population of Asiatic origin from the Middle Kingdom. Bietak's excavations identified its strata.

lugares/napata/resumen.texto: Nubian city beside Jebel Barkal that the Egyptians made the southern frontier of the New Kingdom and the center of the Nubian cult of Amun.

lugares/yebel-barkal/resumen.texto: Sacred mountain of Napata, where Thutmose III built a temple of Amun and which Egypt regarded as the southern limit of its domains.

lugares/soleb/resumen.texto: Temple of Amenhotep III in Nubia, north of the Third Cataract, dedicated to Amun and to the deified king.

lugares/sesebi/resumen.texto: Egyptian city founded by Akhenaten in Nubia, with a temple dedicated to the Aten. It was abandoned shortly after the end of Amarna.

lugares/amara-oeste/resumen.texto: New Kingdom city in Nubia that was the seat of Egyptian government and was abandoned at the end of Egyptian rule.

lugares/kawa/resumen.texto: Site in Nubia with a temple of Amun built by Tutankhamun and later by Taharqa.

lugares/tombos/resumen.texto: Nubian site north of the Third Cataract with an inscription of Thutmose I recording his campaign against Kush.

lugares/dra-abu-el-naga/resumen.texto: Necropolis on the West Bank at Thebes, burial place of kings of the 17th Dynasty and of the first kings of the 18th.

lugares/gurob/resumen.texto: Site in the Fayum with a palace-harem of Thutmose III, from which come administrative papyri and dolls.

lugares/timna/resumen.texto: Copper mining valley in the Negev, worked since the fifth millennium BC, with an Egyptian temple of Hathor from the Ramesside period, c. 1300-1150 BC.

lugares/abu-simbel/resumen.texto: Temples of Ramesses II cut into the rock of Lower Nubia, with the major temple and the minor one dedicated to Nefertari, moved in the 1960s.

lugares/colosos-de-memnon/resumen.texto: Two seated statues of Amenhotep III, about 18 meters high, which are all that remains of the king's mortuary temple on the West Bank at Thebes.

lugares/tell-el-yahudiya/resumen.texto: Fortified site in the Delta with a large earthwork from the Hyksos period and a temple of Ramesses III.

lugares/amada/resumen.texto: Egyptian temple in Nubia founded by Thutmose III and Amenhotep II, moved in the 1960s.

lugares/wadi-es-sebua/resumen.texto: Temple of Ramesses II in Nubia, with an avenue of sphinxes, moved because of Lake Nasser.

lugares/malkata/resumen.texto: Palace complex of Amenhotep III on the West Bank at Thebes, with the palace, temples and a great artificial lake, the Birket Habu, associated with the king's jubilees.

lugares/tt93/resumen.texto: Theban tomb of Kenamun at Sheikh Abd el-Qurna, overseer of the cattle of Amun and steward of Amenhotep II, of the 18th Dynasty. His mother, Amenemipet, was the king's wet nurse, and the tomb preserves more than eighty epithets of Kenamun.

lugares/mazghuna/resumen.texto: Site 5 km south of Dahshur with several mudbrick pyramids of the 12th Dynasty. Amenemhat IV and Sobekneferu have been proposed as the owners of two unfinished pyramids, without conclusive proof; Mackay explored it in 1910 and Petrie excavated it in 1911.

lugares/medinet-madi/resumen.texto: Site in the southwest of the Fayum with the remains of a Graeco-Roman town, where a temple of the harvest cobra goddess Renenutet was founded under Amenemhat III and Amenemhat IV. It was enlarged later, in the Graeco-Roman period.

lugares/biahmu/resumen.texto: Village and site in the Fayum 7 km from the town of El Fayum, with the Pedestals of Biahmu, the ruins of two colossi of Amenemhat III.

lugares/wah-sut/resumen.texto: Town south of Abydos that the state created to house those who worked on the funerary complex of Sesostris III. Kings of the 13th Dynasty and of the Second Intermediate Period, now called the Abydos Dynasty, were later buried beside the tomb of Sesostris III.

lugares/kumma/resumen.texto: 12th-Dynasty fortress in Nubia, also called East Semna, which Sesostris III built together with Semna to protect the southern frontier, about 365 km from Aswan.

lugares/shalfak/resumen.texto: Fortress on the west bank of the Second Cataract, now on an island in Lake Nasser; one of the seventeen that the kings of the 12th Dynasty set up to secure the southern frontier, from Sesostris III onward.

lugares/dabenarti/resumen.texto: Nile island near the Second Cataract, 900 m from Mirgissa and 5 km south of Buhen, with an Egyptian fortress whose construction began under Sesostris I and finished under Sesostris III.

lugares/wadi-el-hudi/resumen.texto: Mining region of the eastern desert, southeast of Aswan, known for its amethyst quarries and for its rock inscriptions, stelae, settlements and mines, mostly dating from the Middle Kingdom.

lugares/gebel-zeit/resumen.texto: Mining area on the Red Sea coast, south of Ras Gharib, to which expeditions were sent from Coptos in the Middle and New Kingdoms; Amenemhat III sent them to extract galena.

lugares/ain-sokhna/resumen.texto: Ancient Egyptian port and settlement on the west bank of the Gulf of Suez, comparable to Mersa Gawasis. In the Middle Kingdom activity continued along the Red Sea and toward the mining areas of Sinai.

lugares/medamud/resumen.texto: Site about 8 km northeast of Luxor where there was a temple of Montu, god of war, excavated by Bisson de la Roque in 1925.

lugares/armant/resumen.texto: Town about 19 km south of Thebes, important in the Middle Kingdom and enlarged in the 18th Dynasty. Mentuhotep II is the earliest builder known with certainty of its temple of Montu.

lugares/kanisah-kurgus/resumen.texto: Site in Sudan on the east bank of the Nile between the Fourth and Fifth Cataracts, with Hagar el-Merwa, a rock art site with border stelae of Thutmose I and Thutmose III. It marks the southern limit of ancient Egypt on the Nile under those kings.

lugares/sai/resumen.texto: Large Nile island in Nubia, between the Second and Third Cataracts, which was an important center of the Kerma kingdom before becoming a major center of Egyptian administration in Kush in the New Kingdom. There is Egyptian activity under Ahmose I, Amenhotep I and Thutmose I, and a larger fortified settlement under Thutmose III, after the defeat of Kerma.

lugares/doukki-gel/resumen.texto: Ancient Nubian settlement less than 1 km south of Kerma, inhabited from c. 1800 BC and occupied by the rulers of Kerma around 1700 BC, and later by Egyptian and Nubian officials in the New Kingdom.

lugares/faras/resumen.texto: Major city of Lower Nubia, now beneath Lake Nasser, which during Egyptian rule was an administrative center with strong Egyptian cultural influence. A Polish mission led by Michałowski found Egyptian temples and Meroitic and Christian cemeteries.

lugares/ellesyia/resumen.texto: Small rock-cut temple near Qasr Ibrim, which Thutmose III dedicated to Horus of Miam, Satis and Amun; it was moved to the Egyptian Museum in Turin because of the rising waters of Lake Nasser.

lugares/beit-el-wali/resumen.texto: Rock-cut temple in Nubia that Ramesses II dedicated to Amun-Ra, Ra-Horakhty, Khnum and Anukis; it was the first of the series of temples he built in the region. It was moved in the 1960s.

lugares/gerf-hussein/resumen.texto: Temple of Ptah dedicated to Ramesses II, built by the viceroy Setau about 90 km south of Aswan, partly freestanding and partly rock-cut. It was moved in the international campaign of the 1960s.

lugares/derr/resumen.texto: Rock-cut temple of Ramesses II from the 19th Dynasty, the only one of his in Nubia on the east bank of the Nile; today it stands at New Amada, in Lower Nubia.

lugares/wadi-allaqi/resumen.texto: Large dry wadi in the eastern desert of southern Egypt, which opens south of Aswan, famous for its gold and its rock inscriptions. A stela attributed to Ramesses II, found near Quban, tells of the search for water for the gold workers.

lugares/speos-artemidos/resumen.texto: Rock-cut temple 2 km south of Beni Hasan, in an ancient limestone quarry, dedicated to the goddess Pakhet, protector and huntress. It was commissioned by Hatshepsut, and it is the earliest known rock temple.

lugares/sala-de-las-fiestas-de-tutmosis-.texto: Sanctuary at the heart of the precinct of Amun-Ra at Karnak, whose name means “the most glorious of monuments”. Thutmose III had the Karnak King List carved there.

lugares/templo-funerario-de-amenhotep-ii.texto: Mortuary Temple of Amenhotep III (Kom el-Hettan)

Mortuary temple of Amenhotep III on the west bank of Thebes, opposite Luxor, built by his architect Amenhotep and the largest funerary complex of its time. Merneptah later built his own with stones from this one.

lugares/templo-de-amenhotep-iv/nombre.texto: Temple of Amenhotep IV at Karnak

lugares/templo-de-amenhotep-iv/resumen.texto: Monument at Karnak used in the first four years of Amenhotep IV's reign, when he had not yet changed his name. It may have been begun at the end of the reign of his father, Amenhotep III.

lugares/gran-templo-de-aton/resumen.texto: Temple at Amarna, the former Akhetaten, which was the main cult place of the god Aten during Akhenaten's reign.

lugares/templo-pequeno-de-aton/resumen.texto: Temple of the Aten in the center of Amarna, next to the King's House and the Royal Palace, originally called the Mansion of the Aten. It is one of the two main temples of the city.

lugares/tumba-real-de-akenaton/resumen.texto: Multi-chambered tomb in the Royal Wadi, east of Amarna, where members of the royal family of the Amarna period were originally buried. It was rediscovered in the 1880s.

lugares/tumbas-de-los-nobles-de-amarna/n.texto: Tombs of the Nobles at Amarna

lugares/tumbas-de-los-nobles-de-amarna/r.texto: Tombs of courtiers and powerful people of Akhetaten, in two groups cut into the cliffs east of the dry bay. There are twenty-five main tombs, many of them decorated and bearing the name of their owner.

lugares/kv20/resumen.texto: Probably the first royal tomb in the Valley of the Kings. It was the original burial of Thutmose I, who was later moved to KV38, and Hatshepsut adapted it for herself and her father.

lugares/kv38/resumen.texto: Tomb in the Valley of the Kings where Thutmose I was reburied; Thutmose III moved him there from KV20. He was later taken to the royal cache at Deir el-Bahari.

lugares/kv39/resumen.texto: High tomb in the cliffs of the Valley of the Kings, far from the valley floor and the other royal burials, which is one of the possible locations of the tomb of Amenhotep I.

lugares/kv34/resumen.texto: Tomb of Thutmose III in the Valley of the Kings, plundered in antiquity and of lost location, which Loret rediscovered and excavated in 1898.

lugares/kv42/resumen.texto: Tomb in the Valley of the Kings built for Hatshepsut-Meryetre, wife of Thutmose III, who was not buried in it. Sennefer, mayor of Thebes under Amenhotep II, may have reused it with several of his relatives.

lugares/kv35/resumen.texto: Tomb of Amenhotep II in the Valley of the Kings, which later served as a cache for other royal mummies. Victor Loret discovered it in March 1898.

lugares/kv43/resumen.texto: Tomb of Thutmose IV in the Valley of the Kings, where he was buried with two of his sons who died before him. It has the bent-axis plan typical of the tombs of the early 18th Dynasty.

lugares/wv22/resumen.texto: Tomb of Amenhotep III in the western branch of the Valley of the Kings, unique for having two secondary burial chambers for his wives Tiye and Sitamun, who was also his daughter.

lugares/kv46/resumen.texto: Tomb of the noble Yuya and his wife Tjuyu, parents of Queen Tiye, in the Valley of the Kings. It was discovered in February 1905 by James E. Quibell, who was excavating for Theodore Davis.

lugares/kv55/resumen.texto: Tomb in the Valley of the Kings that Edward Ayrton found in 1907. For a long time there has been debate over whether the body it contained is that of Akhenaten; genetic and other studies have been cited in that debate.

lugares/kv57/resumen.texto: Royal tomb of Horemheb, last pharaoh of the 18th Dynasty, at the bottom of the Valley of the Kings. Edward Ayrton found it in February 1908, and it was full of debris.

lugares/kv36/resumen.texto: Tomb of Maiherpri, a noble of the 18th Dynasty, in the Valley of the Kings. Victor Loret rediscovered it on 30 March 1899.

lugares/tt8/resumen.texto: Funerary chapel and burial of the foreman Kha and his wife Merit in the north cemetery of the workmen's village of Deir el-Medina. The burial chamber was found intact in 1906, and its burial equipment numbers more than 460 objects.

lugares/tt100/resumen.texto: Funerary chapel of the vizier Rekhmire at Sheikh Abd el-Qurna, in the Theban necropolis. It has no burial chamber beside the chapel; the vizier's burial is elsewhere.

lugares/tt192/resumen.texto: Tomb of Kheruef, also called Senaa, steward of the Great Royal Wife Tiye under Amenhotep III, in El-Assasif, part of the Theban necropolis.

lugares/serapeo-de-saqqara/resumen.texto: Burial place of the sacred Apis bulls of Memphis, which were believed to be incarnations of the god Ptah and became immortal at death as Osiris-Apis. The name of Serapis derives from it.

lugares/tjaru/resumen.texto: Ancient Egyptian fortress on the Way of Horus, the main military route leaving Egypt for Canaan, called Selē in Greek. Reliefs of Thutmose II, Seti I and Ramesses II were found there, and the Amarna Letters mention it as Silu.

lugares/tell-el-borg/resumen.texto: Ancient military settlement in northern Sinai, on the Way of Horus, part of the defensive network guarding Egypt's eastern frontier.

lugares/tell-er-retaba/resumen.texto: Archaeological site in the eastern Delta, in the Wadi Tumilat, whose oldest objects date from the 9th and 12th Dynasties.

lugares/deir-el-balah/resumen.texto: Site in the Gaza Strip; the modern town is about 14 km south of Gaza. From the mid-14th century BC, in the Late Bronze Age, it was a fortified outpost of the New Kingdom of Egypt.

lugares/kamid-el-loz/resumen.texto: Site in the western valley of the Beqaa, in Lebanon, identified with the city of Kumidi of the Amarna Letters.

lugares/osireion/resumen.texto: Cenotaph believed to belong to Seti I, located behind the temple of Seti I at Abydos. Its date is thought to be the same as that of the temple, the 13th century BC.

lugares/templo-funerario-de-seti-i/resum.texto: Memorial temple of Seti I in the Theban necropolis, in Upper Egypt, opposite modern Luxor.

lugares/kv17/resumen.texto: Tomb of Seti I in the Valley of the Kings, one of the largest, deepest and most elaborately decorated in the valley.

lugares/kv7/resumen.texto: Tomb of Ramesses II in the main wadi of the Valley of the Kings, opposite KV5, that of his sons, and near KV8, that of his son and successor Merneptah.

lugares/kv5/nombre.texto: KV5 (Tomb of the Sons of Ramesses II)

lugares/kv5/resumen.texto: Rock-cut tomb in the Valley of the Kings that belonged to the sons of Ramesses II. Part of it was excavated in 1825; its full extent was discovered in 1995 by Kent R. Weeks and his team. It is the largest known tomb in the valley.

lugares/templo-funerario-de-merenptah/re.texto: Mortuary temple of Merneptah in the Theban necropolis, near Kurna. It stands at the northwest end of the mortuary temple of Amenhotep III and was built almost entirely with stones from that temple.

lugares/kv8/resumen.texto: Tomb of Merneptah in the Valley of the Kings, with a burial chamber at the end of a 160 m corridor, which held a set of four nested sarcophagi.

lugares/kv15/resumen.texto: Tomb of Seti II in the Valley of the Kings, cut into the base of an almost vertical cliff at the head of a wadi.

lugares/kv47/resumen.texto: Tomb of Siptah in the Valley of the Kings, which Edward Ayrton found on 18 December 1905, when the king's mummy had already come to light in the KV35 cache.

lugares/kv14/resumen.texto: Joint tomb that Tausert used first and Setnakht reused and enlarged; it had been open since antiquity. Hartwig Altenmüller excavated it from 1983 to 1987.

lugares/kv13/resumen.texto: Tomb in the Valley of the Kings cut and decorated for the 19th-Dynasty noble Bay. An ostracon published in 2000 says that the chancellor Bay was executed by Siptah.

lugares/tumba-de-nefertari/resumen.texto: Tomb of Nefertari, Great Royal Wife of Ramesses II, in the Valley of the Queens, which Ernesto Schiaparelli discovered in 1904. Her name means “the most beautiful of them”.

lugares/templo-de-khonsu/resumen.texto: Temple dedicated to the moon god Khonsu, son of Amun and Mut, in the southwest sector of the precinct of Amun-Ra at Karnak, in Thebes.

lugares/kv11/resumen.texto: Tomb of Ramesses III in the main valley of the Valley of the Kings. Setnakht began it and abandoned it when he accidentally cut into the earlier tomb of Amenmesse (KV10). Setnakht was buried in KV14.

lugares/kv2/resumen.texto: Tomb of Ramesses IV in the lower part of the main valley, between KV7 and KV1, open since antiquity and with many graffiti.

lugares/kv9/nombre.texto: KV9 (Tomb of Ramesses V and VI)

lugares/kv9/resumen.texto: Tomb built by Ramesses V, where he was buried, and which his uncle Ramesses VI reused as his own. Its plan is typical of the 20th Dynasty and much simpler than that of the earlier tombs.

lugares/kv1/resumen.texto: Tomb of Ramesses VII in the Valley of the Kings, open since antiquity and only recently investigated and cleared by Edwin Brock in 1984 and 1985.

lugares/kv6/resumen.texto: Final resting place of Ramesses IX. Archaeological evidence and the uneven quality of the decoration indicate that it was not finished in time for his death and was completed in haste.

lugares/kv18/resumen.texto: Tomb planned for Ramesses X in the Valley of the Kings, abandoned unfinished and not used for his burial.

lugares/kv4/resumen.texto: Tomb begun for Ramesses XI, whose work was abandoned without being used for his burial. Pinedjem I probably considered appropriating it for himself.

lugares/kv3/resumen.texto: Tomb in the Valley of the Kings planned for an unidentified son of Ramesses III at the beginning of the 20th Dynasty; it follows the straight-axis design typical of that dynasty.

lugares/qv44/resumen.texto: One of the tombs in the Valley of the Queens intended for the sons of Ramesses III, with painted reliefs showing the ritual and symbolic journey of Khaemwaset through the afterlife.

lugares/qv55/resumen.texto: Tomb in the Valley of the Queens, in the Theban necropolis, built for Prince Amenherkhepeshef, son of Ramesses III, of the 20th Dynasty.

lugares/elkab/resumen.texto: Site in Upper Egypt on the east bank of the Nile, about 80 km south of Luxor, with prehistoric and Egyptian settlements, rock-cut tombs from the early 18th Dynasty, and temples from the archaic to the Ptolemaic period. It holds the tombs of the rulers of Nekheb, such as Sobeknakht II, Ahmose son of Ebana and Ahmose Pennekhbet.
